-- | The mechanical half of recursive descent: a token cursor with peek,
-- advance, and expect, and a Pratt driver over a binding-power table.
--
-- Deliberately not a combinator library. There is no alternation operator, no
-- backtracking engine, no grammar vocabulary; a caller writes the grammar by
-- hand, in ordinary functions, and hands this module the two things a
-- hand-written parser gets subtly wrong. The first is span arithmetic: joining
-- two spans, covering a consumed run, and pointing a caret at a position where
-- nothing was read. The second is expectation merging: unmet expectations join
-- a set held at the furthest token the cursor ever reached, so a refusal names
-- every alternative tried at the position the parse died at rather than only
-- the last one attempted. Rewinding is where that record is classically lost,
-- so rewinding is a named operation (`cursor_restore`) that returns the
-- position and keeps the record.
--
-- Expectations are token wire names, the vocabulary of `Syntax.Token`, and a
-- refusal renders as a `Syntax.Diagnostic` under the compiler's own parse
-- codes. A parser built on this cursor therefore reports through the same
-- document every other syntax fault does, with no error type of its own.

import Data.List (..)

import Data.Maybe (..)

import Data.String (..)

import Syntax.Source (..)

import Syntax.Token (..)

import Syntax.Diagnostic (..)

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Span arithmetic
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- | The smallest span covering both: the earlier start and the later end. The
-- one operation a parser needs to give a node built from parts the extent of
-- those parts.
--
-- ```prism
-- let s = span_join(span_at(2), span_at(11))
-- (s.lo, s.hi)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- (2, 11)
-- ```
pub fn span_join(a : Span, b : Span) : Span =
  Span { lo = min(a.lo, b.lo), hi = max(a.hi, b.hi) }

-- | The empty span at a byte offset: the caret a diagnostic points with when it
-- has a position but nothing was consumed there.
--
-- ```prism
-- let s = span_at(12)
-- (s.lo, s.hi)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- (12, 12)
-- ```
pub fn span_at(pos : Int) : Span = Span { lo = pos, hi = pos }

-- | The smallest span covering every span in the list, or None for the empty
-- list. Joining has no identity over spans (the empty span at offset zero is a
-- position, not a neutral element), so the empty case is absent rather than
-- invented.
pub fn span_cover(ss : List(Span)) : Option(Span) =
  match ss of
    Nil => None
    Cons(s, rest) => Some(cover_go(s, rest))

fn cover_go(acc : Span, ss : List(Span)) : Span =
  match ss of
    Nil => acc
    Cons(s, rest) => cover_go(span_join(acc, s), rest)

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- The cursor
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- | A token cursor: the tokens being read, the read position, the byte offset
-- the end-of-input caret points at, and the failure record (the furthest
-- position at which an expectation was recorded, and the names recorded there).
-- The failure record is part of the cursor rather than of a failure value
-- because it must outlive every failure a parse recovers from.
pub type Cursor = Cursor {
  toks: Array(Token),
  pos: Int,
  stop: Int,
  far: Int,
  wanted: List(String)
}

-- | The reply of a cursor step: the value and the advanced cursor, or the
-- cursor alone. A refusal still carries a cursor, because the failure record it
-- accumulated is the part worth reporting.
pub type Reply(a) = Took(a, Cursor) | Stuck(Cursor)

-- | A cursor over a token list. `stop` is the byte offset the end-of-input
-- caret points at, normally the length of the source the tokens were lexed
-- from, so a refusal past the last token still carries a position.
pub fn cursor_of(ts : List(Token), stop : Int) : Cursor =
  Cursor {
    toks = array_of_list(ts),
    pos = 0,
    stop = stop,
    far = 0,
    wanted = Nil
  }

-- | The number of tokens the cursor reads over.
pub fn cursor_count(c : Cursor) : Int = array_len(c.toks)

-- | Whether every token has been consumed.
pub fn cursor_at_end(c : Cursor) : Bool = c.pos >= cursor_count(c)

-- | The token `k` positions ahead of the read position, or None past the end.
pub fn cursor_peek_at(c : Cursor, k : Int) : Option(Token) =
  let i = c.pos + k
  if i >= 0 && i < cursor_count(c) then
    Some(array_get(c.toks, i))
  else
    None

-- | The token at the read position, or None at the end. Peeking never consumes
-- and never records an expectation: a parser that looks before it leaps says
-- what it wanted with `cursor_note`.
pub fn cursor_peek(c : Cursor) : Option(Token) = cursor_peek_at(c, 0)

-- | The kind of the token at the read position, or None at the end.
pub fn cursor_kind(c : Cursor) : Option(TokenKind) =
  match cursor_peek(c) of
    None => None
    Some(t) => Some(t.kind)

-- The span of the token at absolute index `i`, or the end-of-input caret when
-- the index is past the last token.
fn span_index(c : Cursor, i : Int) : Span =
  if i >= 0 && i < cursor_count(c) then
    array_get(c.toks, i).span
  else
    span_at(c.stop)

-- | The span the cursor points at: the next token's span, or the end-of-input
-- caret when the stream is exhausted.
pub fn cursor_span(c : Cursor) : Span = span_index(c, c.pos)

-- | The cursor advanced past one token. At the end this is the identity, so a
-- parser that advances on a token it did not check cannot run off the stream.
pub fn cursor_advance(c : Cursor) : Cursor =
  if cursor_at_end(c) then
    c
  else
    Cursor { ..c, pos = c.pos + 1 }

-- | The span covering the tokens consumed between `saved` and `c`, or the caret
-- at the current position when nothing was consumed. A parser gives a node its
-- extent by saving the cursor before it and asking for the run after it, rather
-- than by joining the spans of its parts by hand and forgetting the delimiters.
pub fn cursor_since(saved : Cursor, c : Cursor) : Span =
  if c.pos <= saved.pos then
    span_at(cursor_span(c).lo)
  else
    span_join(span_index(saved, saved.pos), span_index(c, c.pos - 1))

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Expectations
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- | The name the end of the token stream is expected under. Not a token, so not
-- a token kind, but an expectation like any other.
pub fn end_of_input() : String = "end of input"

fn has_name(xs : List(String), name : String) : Bool =
  match xs of
    Nil => false
    Cons(x, rest) =>
      if x == name then
        true
      else
        has_name(rest, name)

fn add_name(xs : List(String), name : String) : List(String) =
  if has_name(xs, name) then
    xs
  else
    append(xs, [name])

-- | Record `name` as admissible at the read position, consuming nothing.
--
-- The record only ever moves forward. A name recorded past the furthest
-- position reached replaces the set and moves the mark; a name at the furthest
-- position joins the set; a name behind it is dropped. That ordering is the
-- whole point: a parse that tries an alternative, gets three tokens deep and
-- fails, then rewinds, must still report what was wanted three tokens in, not
-- what was wanted at the place it rewound to.
pub fn cursor_note_name(c : Cursor, name : String) : Cursor =
  if c.pos > c.far then
    Cursor { ..c, far = c.pos, wanted = [name] }
  elif c.pos == c.far then
    Cursor { ..c, wanted = add_name(c.wanted, name) }
  else
    c

-- | Record a token kind as admissible at the read position. The name recorded
-- is the kind's wire name, so an expectation set, a token artifact, and a
-- diagnostic's `expected` field all speak one vocabulary.
pub fn cursor_note(c : Cursor, k : TokenKind) : Cursor =
  cursor_note_name(c, kind_name(k))

-- | Consume the next token when its kind is `k`. On a mismatch nothing is
-- consumed and `k` joins the expectation set at this position, so a parser that
-- tries several kinds in turn accumulates all of them: expecting one of a set
-- is spelled as expecting each of its members at one position, never as a
-- separate combinator.
pub fn cursor_expect(c : Cursor, k : TokenKind) : Reply(Token) =
  match cursor_peek(c) of
    None => Stuck(cursor_note(c, k))
    Some(t) =>
      if t.kind == k then
        Took(t, cursor_advance(c))
      else
        Stuck(cursor_note(c, k))

-- | Consume the next token when it is the fixed token spelled `s`.
pub fn cursor_expect_fixed(c : Cursor, s : String) : Reply(Token) =
  cursor_expect(c, TFixed(s))

-- | Require that every token has been consumed, recording the end of the stream
-- as the expectation when one is left over.
pub fn cursor_expect_end(c : Cursor) : Reply(Unit) =
  if cursor_at_end(c) then
    Took((), c)
  else
    Stuck(cursor_note_name(c, end_of_input()))

-- | Rewind to a saved cursor while keeping the failure record reached since.
--
-- A parser that tries an alternative and gives it up restores with this: the
-- position returns, the expectations do not. Rebuilding the saved cursor by
-- hand instead is the classic way to report the expectations of the position
-- the parse retreated to rather than of the position it died at.
--
-- ```prism
-- let c0 = cursor_of(Nil, 0)
-- let c1 = cursor_note_name(c0, "ident")
-- str_join(", ", cursor_expected(cursor_restore(c0, c1)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- ident
-- ```
pub fn cursor_restore(saved : Cursor, c : Cursor) : Cursor =
  Cursor { ..saved, far = c.far, wanted = c.wanted }

-- | The names recorded at the furthest position reached, in the order they were
-- first recorded.
--
-- ```prism
-- let c = cursor_note_name(cursor_of(Nil, 3), "ident")
-- str_join(", ", cursor_expected(cursor_note_name(c, "int")))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- ident, int
-- ```
pub fn cursor_expected(c : Cursor) : List(String) = c.wanted

-- Insert one name into a sorted, deduplicated list.
fn ins_name(n : String, acc : List(String)) : List(String) =
  match acc of
    Nil => [n]
    Cons(h, t) =>
      if n < h then
        Cons(n, acc)
      elif n == h then
        acc
      else
        Cons(h, ins_name(n, t))

-- | The canonical expectation set of a refusal: the recorded names
-- deduplicated and byte-lexicographically sorted, so the set a diagnostic
-- carries does not depend on the order alternatives were tried, and a
-- harmless reordering of a parser's branches moves no artifact bytes.
--
-- ```prism
-- let c = cursor_note_name(cursor_of(Nil, 3), "int")
-- str_join(", ", cursor_canonical(cursor_note_name(c, "ident")))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- ident, int
-- ```
pub fn cursor_canonical(c : Cursor) : List(String) = foldr(ins_name, [], c.wanted)

-- | The span the failure record points at: the token at the furthest position
-- reached, or the end-of-input caret.
pub fn cursor_far_span(c : Cursor) : Span = span_index(c, c.far)

-- The wire name of the token the failure record points at, for a message.
fn found_name(c : Cursor) : String =
  if c.far >= cursor_count(c) then
    end_of_input()
  else
    kind_name(array_get(c.toks, c.far).kind)

-- | The rendered message of an unmet expectation: the merged expectation set
-- and what stood there instead.
pub fn cursor_message(c : Cursor) : String =
  let found = found_name(c)
  match c.wanted of
    Nil => "unexpected {found}"
    Cons(x, rest) =>
      match rest of
        Nil => "expected {x}, found {found}"
        Cons(_, _) =>
          let all = str_join(", ", c.wanted)
          "expected one of {all}, found {found}"

-- | The compiler's general parse-fault code, the one home for the string on
-- this side of the seam.
pub fn parse_syntax_code() : String = "E7100"

-- | The compiler's exhausted-stream code: the token stream itself ended while
-- the parser wanted more.
pub fn parse_eof_code() : String = "E7101"

-- | The stable code an unmet expectation carries: the parser's end-of-input
-- code when the furthest position reached is past the last token, and its
-- general syntax code otherwise. Both match the compiler's own parse codes.
pub fn cursor_code(c : Cursor) : String =
  if c.far >= cursor_count(c) then
    parse_eof_code()
  else
    parse_syntax_code()

-- | The refusal an unmet expectation produces: a parse-phase diagnostic at the
-- furthest position reached, carrying the canonical expectation set. The
-- message keeps the order alternatives were tried, for a reader; the set is
-- sorted, for the artifact. A cursor failure is a diagnostic and never a
-- bespoke error value, so a hand-written parser's refusals join the same
-- document the compiler's own do.
pub fn cursor_diagnostic(c : Cursor) : Diagnostic =
  Diagnostic {
    code = cursor_code(c),
    phase = DPParse,
    span = cursor_far_span(c),
    message = cursor_message(c),
    expected = cursor_canonical(c),
    related = Nil
  }

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- The Pratt driver
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------

-- | How an infix operator groups a chain of its own level. A non-associative
-- operator declines a second application at its level, leaving the second
-- operator unconsumed for the caller to refuse.
pub type Assoc = ALeft | ARight | ANone deriving (Eq)

-- | One infix operator: the token spelling, its level (higher binds tighter),
-- and how it associates.
pub type Infix = Infix { op: String, level: Int, assoc: Assoc }

-- | One prefix operator: the token spelling and the level its operand is
-- parsed at. An operator that binds tighter than that level is pulled into the
-- operand; one that binds looser takes the prefix application as its left
-- operand.
pub type Prefix = Prefix { op: String, level: Int }

-- | The power binding an infix operator's left operand.
--
-- Levels are doubled so each has a half step above it. A left-associative
-- operator's right power sits in that half step, which stops a second operator
-- of the same level from being pulled into the right operand; a right
-- associative operator's left power sits there instead, which lets it be. A
-- non-associative operator is left-shaped here and refuses the repeat outright.
pub fn infix_left_bp(i : Infix) : Int =
  match i.assoc of
    ARight => i.level * 2 + 1
    _ => i.level * 2

-- | The power an infix operator's right operand is parsed at.
pub fn infix_right_bp(i : Infix) : Int =
  match i.assoc of
    ARight => i.level * 2
    _ => i.level * 2 + 1

-- | The power a prefix operator's operand is parsed at.
pub fn prefix_bp(p : Prefix) : Int = p.level * 2

-- | The entry for an operator spelling in an infix table, or None when the
-- spelling is not an infix operator.
pub fn infix_lookup(tbl : List(Infix), op : String) : Option(Infix) =
  match tbl of
    Nil => None
    Cons(i, rest) =>
      if i.op == op then
        Some(i)
      else
        infix_lookup(rest, op)

-- | The entry for an operator spelling in a prefix table, or None when the
-- spelling is not a prefix operator.
pub fn prefix_lookup(tbl : List(Prefix), op : String) : Option(Prefix) =
  match tbl of
    Nil => None
    Cons(p, rest) =>
      if p.op == op then
        Some(p)
      else
        prefix_lookup(rest, op)

-- | Everything the driver needs that is not the cursor: the two operator
-- tables, the leaf parser, and the two node builders. The leaf parser owns
-- primaries, and so owns parentheses, and so owns the recursion back into the
-- driver: the driver knows about operators and nothing else.
pub type Pratt(a) = Pratt {
  infixes: List(Infix),
  prefixes: List(Prefix),
  leaf: (Cursor) -> Reply(a),
  bin: (String, a, a) -> a,
  pre: (String, a) -> a
}

-- The fixed-token spelling of the token at the read position, or None when the
-- next token is not a fixed token (a literal or an identifier is never an
-- operator).
fn spelling_at(c : Cursor) : Option(String) =
  match cursor_peek(c) of
    None => None
    Some(t) =>
      match t.kind of
        TFixed(s) => Some(s)
        _ => None

fn prefix_at(sp : Pratt(a), c : Cursor) : Option(Prefix) =
  match spelling_at(c) of
    None => None
    Some(s) => prefix_lookup(sp.prefixes, s)

fn infix_at(sp : Pratt(a), c : Cursor) : Option(Infix) =
  match spelling_at(c) of
    None => None
    Some(s) => infix_lookup(sp.infixes, s)

-- One operand: a prefix operator applied to an operand parsed at the prefix's
-- own power, or a leaf. The prefix table is consulted first because at operand
-- position a spelling that is both prefix and infix (`-`) is the prefix one.
fn pratt_operand(sp : Pratt(a), c : Cursor) : Reply(a) =
  match prefix_at(sp, c) of
    None => (sp.leaf)(c)
    Some(p) =>
      match pratt_expr(sp, cursor_advance(c), prefix_bp(p)) of
        Stuck(c2) => Stuck(c2)
        Took(x, c2) => Took((sp.pre)(p.op, x), c2)

-- The operator loop. `blocked` is the level of the non-associative operator
-- just reduced, or -1: a second operator of that level is declined rather than
-- consumed, which is how `a == b == c` stops after `a == b`. Any other
-- reduction clears the block, so `a == b || c == d` is unaffected.
fn pratt_loop(
  sp : Pratt(a),
  lhs : a,
  c : Cursor,
  min_bp : Int,
  blocked : Int
) : Reply(a) =
  match infix_at(sp, c) of
    None => Took(lhs, c)
    Some(ix) =>
      let repeat = ix.assoc == ANone && ix.level == blocked
      if infix_left_bp(ix) < min_bp || repeat then
        Took(lhs, c)
      else
        match pratt_expr(sp, cursor_advance(c), infix_right_bp(ix)) of
          Stuck(c2) => Stuck(c2)
          Took(rhs, c2) =>
            let next =
              if ix.assoc == ANone then
                ix.level
              else
                -1
            pratt_loop(sp, (sp.bin)(ix.op, lhs, rhs), c2, min_bp, next)

-- | Parse one expression whose operators all bind at least as tightly as
-- `min_bp`: one operand, then every operator that outbinds the caller.
pub fn pratt_expr(sp : Pratt(a), c : Cursor, min_bp : Int) : Reply(a) =
  match pratt_operand(sp, c) of
    Stuck(c2) => Stuck(c2)
    Took(lhs, c2) => pratt_loop(sp, lhs, c2, min_bp, -1)

-- | Parse one expression at the loosest binding power. Tokens after it are left
-- for the caller, which is what makes this usable inside a larger grammar.
pub fn pratt_parse(sp : Pratt(a), c : Cursor) : Reply(a) = pratt_expr(sp, c, 0)

-- | Parse one expression and require the whole token stream to be consumed. A
-- trailing operator the driver declined (a repeated non-associative one) is
-- refused here, at the position it stands.
pub fn pratt_all(sp : Pratt(a), c : Cursor) : Reply(a) =
  match pratt_parse(sp, c) of
    Stuck(c2) => Stuck(c2)
    Took(x, c2) =>
      match cursor_expect_end(c2) of
        Stuck(c3) => Stuck(c3)
        Took(_, c3) => Took(x, c3)

-- | The infix table of Prism's own expression grammar, loosest first. Levels
-- are relative: only their order and each operator's associativity carry
-- meaning, and both are pinned against the compiler's parser by a differential
-- test rather than by this comment.
pub fn expr_infix_table() : List(Infix) =
  [
      Infix { op = "??", level = 1, assoc = ARight },
      Infix { op = "|>", level = 2, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = ">>", level = 3, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "<<", level = 3, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "||", level = 4, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "&&", level = 5, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "==", level = 6, assoc = ANone },
      Infix { op = "/=", level = 6, assoc = ANone },
      Infix { op = "<", level = 6, assoc = ANone },
      Infix { op = "<=", level = 6, assoc = ANone },
      Infix { op = ">", level = 6, assoc = ANone },
      Infix { op = ">=", level = 6, assoc = ANone },
      Infix { op = "+", level = 7, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "-", level = 7, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "*", level = 8, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "/", level = 8, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "%", level = 8, assoc = ALeft },
      Infix { op = "^", level = 10, assoc = ARight },
    ]

-- | The prefix table of Prism's own expression grammar: unary minus, sitting
-- between multiplication and exponentiation. `-x * y` is `(-x) * y` and, by the
-- mathematical convention, `-x ^ y` is `-(x ^ y)`.
pub fn expr_prefix_table() : List(Prefix) = [Prefix { op = "-", level = 9 }]

-- | The typed vocabulary of the `prism-syntax-diagnostics-v1` artifact.
--
-- One document per source file: the embedded source identity and every
-- syntax-boundary diagnostic the lexer or parser produced for it, in source
-- order. An accepted file carries the empty list, so acceptance and refusal
-- share one shape. `expected` and `related` are reserved surfaces: always
-- present, possibly empty, so a reader written today survives their arrival.

import Syntax.Source (..)

-- | The phase that raised a diagnostic.
pub type DiagPhase = DPLex | DPParse

-- | One diagnostic: the stable append-only code, the raising phase, the
-- primary half-open byte span (a lex fault is a caret, `lo == hi`), the
-- rendered message, the parser's canonical expectation set when it has one,
-- and related spans.
pub type Diagnostic = Diagnostic {
  code: String,
  phase: DiagPhase,
  span: Span,
  message: String,
  expected: List(String),
  related: List(Span)
}

-- | A decoded diagnostics document: the envelope identity, the embedded
-- source every span indexes into, and the diagnostics in source order.
pub type DiagnosticsDoc = DiagnosticsDoc {
  schema: String,
  compiler: String,
  source: SourceFile,
  diagnostics: List(Diagnostic)
}

-- | The schema tag this vocabulary decodes.
pub fn diagnostics_schema() : String = "prism-syntax-diagnostics-v1"

-- | Whether the document accepted its source (no diagnostics).
pub fn doc_accepted(d : DiagnosticsDoc) : Bool =
  match d.diagnostics of
    Nil => true
    Cons(_, _) => false

Span-addressed source edits that refuse rather than corrupt.

An edit is a byte span and its replacement text, which is the only edit vocabulary a tool built on the syntax seams needs: every artifact those seams publish addresses source by exact byte span, so a tool that computes spans can state its whole result as a list of them without ever holding a mutable buffer.

The apply step is where the guarantee lives. Edits are sorted by start offset (a stable sort, so two edits at the same offset keep the order the caller gave them), a span that runs backwards or past the end is refused, overlapping edits are refused, and the spliced result is re-lexed before it is returned. An edit set that would produce a file the lexer cannot read comes back as a structured refusal naming the lexer's own error, never as a corrupt file. That is the difference between a rename tool and a search-and-replace: this one fails closed.

The re-lex is a lexical check and nothing more. It catches an edit that unbalances a string, a hole, or a numeric literal; it does not claim the result parses, typechecks, or means what the caller intended.
modules.source:
-- | Span-addressed source edits that refuse rather than corrupt.
--
-- An edit is a byte span and its replacement text, which is the only edit
-- vocabulary a tool built on the syntax seams needs: every artifact those seams
-- publish addresses source by exact byte span, so a tool that computes spans can
-- state its whole result as a list of them without ever holding a mutable
-- buffer.
--
-- The apply step is where the guarantee lives. Edits are sorted by start offset
-- (a stable sort, so two edits at the same offset keep the order the caller gave
-- them), a span that runs backwards or past the end is refused, overlapping
-- edits are refused, and the spliced result is re-lexed before it is returned.
-- An edit set that would produce a file the lexer cannot read comes back as a
-- structured refusal naming the lexer's own error, never as a corrupt file. That
-- is the difference between a rename tool and a search-and-replace: this one
-- fails closed.
--
-- The re-lex is a lexical check and nothing more. It catches an edit that
-- unbalances a string, a hole, or a numeric literal; it does not claim the
-- result parses, typechecks, or means what the caller intended.

import Data.Foldable (length)

import Data.List (foldl)

import Syntax.Lex (..)

import Syntax.Source (..)

-- | One edit: the byte span it replaces and the text that replaces it. An
-- insertion is an empty span, a deletion is empty text.
pub type Edit = Edit { span: Span, text: String }

-- | Why an edit set was refused. Every case names the offending span, so a tool
-- can point at the edit it got wrong.
pub type EditError
  = EdBadSpan(Span)
  | EdPastEnd(Span, Int)
  | EdOverlap(Span, Span)
  | EdRelex(LexError)
  deriving (Eq, Show)

-- | An insertion at one offset.
pub fn ed_insert_at(offset : Int, text : String) : Edit =
  Edit {
    span = Span { lo = offset, hi = offset },
    text = text
  }

-- | A deletion of one span.
pub fn ed_delete(span : Span) : Edit = Edit { span = span, text = "" }

-- | A replacement of one span.
pub fn ed_replace(span : Span, text : String) : Edit =
  Edit { span = span, text = text }

-- | The current text under a span, or `None` when the span does not address
-- this text. What a rename reads to check that an occurrence still says what the
-- plan assumed.
pub fn ed_span_text(text : String, s : Span) : Option(String) =
  if span_valid(s) && s.hi <= str_len(text) then
    Some(substring(text, s.lo, span_len(s)))
  else
    None

-- | A human-readable account of a refusal.
pub fn ed_message(e : EditError) : String =
  match e of
    EdBadSpan(s) => "edit span {show(s.lo)}..{show(s.hi)} is not well formed"
    EdPastEnd(s, n) =>
      "edit span {show(s.lo)}..{show(s.hi)} runs past the end of {show(n)} bytes"
    EdOverlap(a, b) =>
      "edits {show(a.lo)}..{show(a.hi)} and {show(b.lo)}..{show(b.hi)} overlap"
    EdRelex(le) => "the edited text does not lex: {lex_message(le)}"

-- | The edits sorted by start offset, stably: two edits starting at the same
-- offset keep their input order, so a caller that means "insert A then B here"
-- gets it.
pub fn ed_sort(edits : List(Edit)) : List(Edit) = foldl(ed_place, Nil, edits)

fn ed_place(sorted : List(Edit), e : Edit) : List(Edit) =
  match sorted of
    Nil => [e]
    Cons(x, rest) =>
      if x.span.lo <= e.span.lo then
        Cons(x, ed_place(rest, e))
      else
        Cons(e, sorted)

-- | Apply an edit set to a source text.
--
-- The result is the spliced text when every edit is well formed, the edits do
-- not overlap, and the splice still lexes. Otherwise it is the first refusal
-- found, in that order.
pub fn ed_apply(text : String, edits : List(Edit)) : Result(String, EditError) =
  match ed_splice(text, ed_sort(edits), 0, None, "") of
    Err(e) => Err(e)
    Ok(out) => ed_relex(out)

-- | How many edits an edit set holds: the count a plan reports before anything
-- is applied.
pub fn ed_count(edits : List(Edit)) : Int = length(edits)

fn ed_relex(out : String) : Result(String, EditError) =
  match lex_raw(out) of
    Err(le) => Err(EdRelex(le))
    Ok(_) => Ok(out)

fn ed_splice(
  text : String,
  edits : List(Edit),
  at : Int,
  prev : Option(Span),
  acc : String
) : Result(String, EditError) =
  match edits of
    Nil => Ok(concat(acc, substring(text, at, str_len(text) - at)))
    Cons(e, rest) =>
      if not(span_valid(e.span)) then
        Err(EdBadSpan(e.span))
      elif e.span.hi > str_len(text) then
        Err(EdPastEnd(e.span, str_len(text)))
      elif e.span.lo < at then
        Err(EdOverlap(ed_prev_span(prev, e.span), e.span))
      else
        ed_splice(
            text,
            rest,
            e.span.hi,
            Some(e.span),
            concat(concat(acc, substring(text, at, e.span.lo - at)), e.text),
          )

fn ed_prev_span(prev : Option(Span), here : Span) : Span =
  match prev of
    Some(s) => s
    None => here

modules.doc:
Call-graph flow over a resolved document: occurrence analysis and liveness as one fixpoint.

The questions a compiler asks about a call graph (what does this function transitively reach, which functions are reachable from the entry points, which ones recurse) are one program with three settings of the same three knobs: a per-node contribution, a join, and a dependency relation. `Data.Fixpoint` solves that program; this module supplies the three knobs from the `prism-resolved-syntax-v1` document, so the analysis runs over a real resolved tree rather than a hand-built graph. Transitive reach propagates along the calls relation; liveness is the identical solve with the relation reversed and a Boolean carrier.

The edges come from the same seam `Syntax.Rename` queries, with the same limit. A `var` node's span covers exactly its identifier, so every reference is readable, but no reference carries the identity of the binder it resolved to. A local binder spelled like a top-level function is therefore read as a call to that function, which adds edges that are not there. Every answer here is that over-approximation: `fl_dead` names only functions that really are unreachable, and `fl_transitive` may list a callee a run never makes. When the seam grows a binder-identity fact the approximation tightens without an interface change. Opt-in: not in Base.
modules.source:
-- | Call-graph flow over a resolved document: occurrence analysis and liveness
-- as one fixpoint.
--
-- The questions a compiler asks about a call graph (what does this function
-- transitively reach, which functions are reachable from the entry points, which
-- ones recurse) are one program with three settings of the same three knobs:
-- a per-node contribution, a join, and a dependency relation. `Data.Fixpoint`
-- solves that program; this module supplies the three knobs from the
-- `prism-resolved-syntax-v1` document, so the analysis runs over a real resolved
-- tree rather than a hand-built graph. Transitive reach propagates along the
-- calls relation; liveness is the identical solve with the relation reversed and
-- a Boolean carrier.
--
-- The edges come from the same seam `Syntax.Rename` queries, with the same
-- limit. A `var` node's span covers exactly its identifier, so every reference
-- is readable, but no reference carries the identity of the binder it resolved
-- to. A local binder spelled like a top-level function is therefore read as a
-- call to that function, which adds edges that are not there. Every answer here
-- is that over-approximation: `fl_dead` names only functions that really are
-- unreachable, and `fl_transitive` may list a callee a run never makes. When the
-- seam grows a binder-identity fact the approximation tightens without an
-- interface change. Opt-in: not in Base.

import Data.Fixpoint (fix_at, fix_propagate)

import Data.Foldable (elem)

import Data.Graph (graph_add_edge, graph_add_node, graph_empty, graph_reverse, graph_successors)

import Data.List (concat_map, filter, foldl, map)

import Data.Map (map_empty, map_insert, map_keys, map_to_list)

import Data.Set (set_from_list, set_member, set_to_list)

import Syntax.Edit (ed_span_text)

import Syntax.Resolved (..)

import Syntax.Source (..)

-- | The names the document defines, as a set.
pub fn fl_defined(doc : ResolvedDoc) : Map(String, Unit) =
  set_from_list(map(fl_fn_name, doc.functions))

fn fl_fn_name(f : RFunction) : String = f.name

-- | Every identifier one function's body references, in source order, sliced
-- from the embedded source. A reference the source cannot address is dropped,
-- which `Syntax.Rename`'s `rn_unaddressed` is how to detect before trusting any
-- answer here.
pub fn fl_references(src : SourceFile, f : RFunction) : List(String) =
  concat_map(\(n) -> fl_reference(src, n), rnode_universe(f.body))

fn fl_reference(src : SourceFile, n : RNode) : List(String) =
  if n.kind == rkind_var() then
    match ed_span_text(src.text, n.span) of
      Some(name) => [name]
      None => []
  else
    []

-- | The call graph: an edge from each function to every function of this
-- document it references. Every defined function is a node, so one that calls
-- nothing still gets an answer, and successor lists are ascending and
-- duplicate-free, so the iteration order below is a function of the document
-- alone.
pub fn fl_calls(doc : ResolvedDoc) : Map(String, List(String)) =
  let defined = fl_defined(doc)
  foldl(
      \(g, f) -> fl_edges(g, doc.source, defined, f),
      graph_empty,
      doc.functions,
    )

fn fl_edges(
  g : Map(String, List(String)),
  src : SourceFile,
  defined : Map(String, Unit),
  f : RFunction
) : Map(String, List(String)) =
  foldl(
      \(a, name) -> graph_add_edge(a, f.name, name),
      graph_add_node(g, f.name),
      filter(\(name) -> set_member(name, defined), fl_references(src, f)),
    )

-- | The immediate successors of a graph as a set per node: the per-node
-- contribution a propagation starts from.
--
-- ```prism
-- # import Data.Graph (..)
-- map(\(p) -> (fst(p), set_to_list(snd(p))), map_to_list(fl_direct(graph_from_edges([("f", "g")]))))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- [(f, [g])]
-- ```
pub fn fl_direct(g : Map(k, List(k))) : Map(k, Map(k, Unit)) given Ord(k) =
  foldl(
      \(acc, key) -> map_insert(key, set_from_list(graph_successors(g, key)), acc),
      map_empty,
      map_keys(g),
    )

-- | Every function each function transitively calls: the least assignment with
-- `x[f]` the union of `direct[f]` and every `x[g]` for `g` in `direct[f]`. The
-- members of one cycle share one answer, and a function on a cycle lists itself.
pub fn fl_transitive(doc : ResolvedDoc) : Map(String, Map(String, Unit)) ! {Fail | e} =
  let calls = fl_calls(doc)
  fix_propagate(fl_direct(calls), calls)

-- | The functions reachable from `roots`: the same solve with the calls relation
-- reversed, so reachability flows from a caller to its callees, over the Boolean
-- lattice. A root the document does not define contributes nothing.
pub fn fl_live(
  doc : ResolvedDoc,
  roots : List(String)
) : Map(String, Unit) ! {Fail | e} =
  let calls = fl_calls(doc)
  let seeds = foldl(
      \(acc, key) -> map_insert(key, elem(key, roots), acc),
      map_empty,
      map_keys(calls),
    )
  fl_reached(fix_propagate(seeds, graph_reverse(calls)))

fn fl_reached(x : Map(String, Bool)) : Map(String, Unit) =
  set_from_list(map(fst, filter(\(p) -> snd(p), map_to_list(x))))

-- | The functions no root reaches, ascending: what a dead-code report is, once
-- the document's entry points are named.
pub fn fl_dead(
  doc : ResolvedDoc,
  roots : List(String)
) : List(String) ! {Fail | e} =
  let live = fl_live(doc, roots)
  filter(\(name) -> not(set_member(name, live)), set_to_list(fl_defined(doc)))

-- | The functions that call themselves, directly or through a cycle, ascending.
-- This is the question a plain traversal answers wrongly and the fixpoint
-- answers by construction: mutual recursion is a cycle, not a self-edge.
pub fn fl_recursive(doc : ResolvedDoc) : List(String) ! {Fail | e} =
  let reach = fl_transitive(doc)
  filter(\(name) -> set_member(name, fix_at(reach, name)), map_keys(reach))

The identities a Prism source file carries, and the two of them a published artifact is enough to compute.

*Source identity* is the exact bytes, comments and formatting included: the digest the compiler embeds in every syntax artifact. *Surface identity* is the canonical semantic surface tree with every source position erased, so a comment or layout edit leaves it fixed while a change of syntactic form moves it. *Core identity* is the elaborated subject and is deliberately not computable here: it needs resolution and elaboration, which no syntax artifact carries.

The negative directions are the essential ones. Equal Core identity does not imply equal surface or source identity, since distinct spellings elaborate to one subject. Equal source bytes do not imply equal Core identity either, because the same text means different things under a different set of imported modules. Nothing here may be read as a claim about behavior.
modules.source:
-- | The identities a Prism source file carries, and the two of them a
-- published artifact is enough to compute.
--
-- *Source identity* is the exact bytes, comments and formatting included: the
-- digest the compiler embeds in every syntax artifact. *Surface identity* is
-- the canonical semantic surface tree with every source position erased, so a
-- comment or layout edit leaves it fixed while a change of syntactic form
-- moves it. *Core identity* is the elaborated subject and is deliberately not
-- computable here: it needs resolution and elaboration, which no syntax
-- artifact carries.
--
-- The negative directions are the essential ones. Equal Core identity does
-- not imply equal surface or source identity, since distinct spellings
-- elaborate to one subject. Equal source bytes do not imply equal Core
-- identity either, because the same text means different things under a
-- different set of imported modules. Nothing here may be read as a claim about
-- behavior.

import Control.Rewrite (..)

import Data.List (filter)

import Data.Result (map_result)

import Json (..)

import Syntax.Codec (..)

import Syntax.Source (..)

-- | The source identity of an artifact: the digest of its exact bytes.
--
-- ```prism
-- # import Syntax.Source (..)
-- source_identity(SourceFile { digest = "9f86d0", text = "fn main() = ()" })
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 9f86d0
-- ```
pub fn source_identity(f : SourceFile) : String = f.digest

-- | The surface identity of a decoded surface document: the canonical rendering
-- of its schema tag and item tree with every span erased.
--
-- Two documents share a surface identity exactly when they are the same tree of
-- the same schema, whatever text produced them. The identity is computed by
-- re-encoding the document and stripping positions from the result, so it
-- inherits the encoder's canonical layout rather than introducing a second one;
-- an encoding that cannot be read back is reported, never silently accepted.
pub fn surface_identity(d : SurfaceDoc) : Result(String, JsonError) =
  map_result(
      \(j) -> canonical_json(surface_subject(j)),
      decode(encode_surface(d)),
    )

-- The identity-bearing part of an encoded document: the schema tag and the
-- items, positions erased. The embedded source is source identity and the
-- compiler stamp is build identity; neither belongs to the tree's own identity.
fn surface_subject(j : Json) : Json =
  match j of
    JObj(fields) => strip_positions(JObj(filter(is_subject_field, fields)))
    _ => j

fn is_subject_field(kv : (String, Json)) : Bool =
  match kv of
    (k, _) => k == "schema" || k == "items"

fn is_position_field(kv : (String, Json)) : Bool =
  match kv of
    (k, _) => not(k == "span")

-- The rule, stated once and locally: an object loses its span fields, and
-- nothing else here has an opinion. `None` is how a rule says it does not apply.
fn drop_spans(j : Json) : Option(Json) =
  match j of
    JObj(fields) => Some(JObj(filter(is_position_field, fields)))
    _ => None

-- Every position erased, at every depth. The traversal is `rw_everywhere`, so
-- this module states the rule and states nothing about how the tree is walked;
-- dropping a span field drops its subtree with it, whichever order the walk
-- reaches them in.
fn strip_positions(j : Json) : Json = rw_everywhere(json_layer(), drop_spans, j)

The Prism-language reimplementation of the compiler's layout pass: the offside rule that splices the virtual block delimiters.

It turns the raw token stream into the post-layout `parse` stream by splicing `VOpen`/`VClose`/`VSemi` and by opening a bare-indent body after each `class`/`instance`/`effect` head. The Rust `lex` pipeline stays the authoritative oracle; this module reproduces its output so the two can be diffed, never used as a silent fallback.

The pipeline mirrors the compiler exactly: `lex_raw` (Syntax.Lex) yields the decoded raw tokens; `inject` splices a zero-width head opener after every declaration head (the head runs to the last token on the keyword's line); the offside driver walks the injected stream with an indent stack, a bracket depth, and a carried-opener flag, emitting the virtual delimiters at zero-width spans; and the synthetic head openers are dropped from the result. The whole file is one Eager top-level block, opened at the first token and closed at end of input, and a block only opens after an opener that begins a deeper new line (the Conditional opener rule), so a one-line `let x = e` stays flat.
modules.source:
-- | The Prism-language reimplementation of the compiler's layout pass: the
-- offside rule that splices the virtual block delimiters.
--
-- It turns the raw token stream into the post-layout `parse` stream by splicing
-- `VOpen`/`VClose`/`VSemi` and by opening a bare-indent body after each
-- `class`/`instance`/`effect` head. The Rust `lex` pipeline stays the
-- authoritative oracle; this module reproduces its output so the two can be
-- diffed, never used as a silent fallback.
--
-- The pipeline mirrors the compiler exactly: `lex_raw` (Syntax.Lex) yields the
-- decoded raw tokens; `inject` splices a zero-width head opener after every
-- declaration head (the head runs to the last token on the keyword's line); the
-- offside driver walks the injected stream with an indent stack, a bracket
-- depth, and a carried-opener flag, emitting the virtual delimiters at zero-width
-- spans; and the synthetic head openers are dropped from the result. The whole
-- file is one Eager top-level block, opened at the first token and closed at end
-- of input, and a block only opens after an opener that begins a deeper new line
-- (the Conditional opener rule), so a one-line `let x = e` stays flat.

import Data.List (..)

import Data.Maybe (..)

import Data.Result (..)

import Syntax.Source (..)

import Syntax.Token (..)

import Syntax.Lex (..)

-- The offside driver's state: the indent stack (top = head), whether the last
-- opener is still pending a block, whether an opener is being carried across a
-- bracket group, the open-bracket depth, the line of the previous token, and the
-- end offset of the previous token (where a virtual close or separator anchors).
type LState = LState {
  stack: List(Int),
  pending_opener: Bool,
  carrying: Bool,
  bracket_depth: Int,
  prev_line: Option(Int),
  prev_off: Int,
  last_hi: Int
}

-- One entry of the injected stream: a real token, or a synthetic head opener at
-- a zero-width offset (the elided `where` of a declaration body).
type LEntry = LTok(Token) | LHead(Int)

-- The result of one driver step: the new state and the reversed output so far.
type StepR = StepR(LState, List(Token))

-- The result of the virtual-emission phase: the new stack and reversed output,
-- and the recomputed opener and carry flags.
type Ph1R = Ph1R { stack: List(Int), out: List(Token), po: Bool, carry: Bool }

-- The result of the bracket-depth phase: the new depth and the opener and carry
-- flags after a carried opener may have re-armed on a closing bracket.
type Ph2R = Ph2R { depth: Int, po: Bool, carry: Bool }

-- The result of collapsing the indent stack down to a column: the trimmed stack
-- and the reversed output with any closes or separator appended.
type CloseR = CloseR { stack: List(Int), out: List(Token) }

-- One indent-stack action at a fresh line: pop a deeper frame, separate a
-- sibling at the same column, or do nothing.
type Close3 = CPop | CSep | CNone

-- The result of scanning a declaration head: the tokens after the head, the
-- head's end offset, and the reversed entries with the head tokens appended.
type HeadR = HeadR { rest: List(Token), endoff: Int, acc: List(LEntry) }

-- The offset of the first byte of the line containing `off`: scan left to the
-- byte after the previous newline, or the start of input.
fn ly_line_start(text : String, off : Int) : Int =
  var j := off
  while j > 0 && byte_at(text, j - 1) /= 10 do
    j -= 1
  j

-- The column of `off`: its byte distance from the line start. Tabs count as one
-- column and every other byte counts as one, matching the compiler's ordinal
-- (non-display) column used for layout decisions.
fn ly_col(text : String, off : Int) : Int = off - ly_line_start(text, off)

-- The newlines in [a, b): the line increment from `a` to `b`. Entries are
-- scanned in offset order, so the driver advances the line number by the gap it
-- just crossed. Recounting from byte zero at each entry would instead cost
-- entries times bytes.
fn ly_count_nl(text : String, a : Int, b : Int) : Int =
  var i := a
  var c := 0
  while i < b do
    if byte_at(text, i) == 10 then
      c += 1
    i += 1
  c

-- The line `prev_off` sits on: zero before any entry has been seen, which is
-- the line byte zero sits on.
fn ly_prev_line(st : LState) : Int =
  match st.prev_line of
    Some(l) => l
    None => 0

-- The head of an indent stack, or None when empty.
fn ly_top(xs : List(Int)) : Option(Int) =
  match xs of
    Nil => None
    Cons(h, _) => Some(h)

-- The tail of an indent stack.
fn ly_pop(xs : List(Int)) : List(Int) =
  match xs of
    Nil => Nil
    Cons(_, t) => t

-- The number of frames on an indent stack.
fn ly_depth(xs : List(Int)) : Int =
  match xs of
    Nil => 0
    Cons(_, t) => 1 + ly_depth(t)

-- A zero-width virtual token of the given kind at `off`.
fn ly_virt(k : TokenKind, off : Int) : Token =
  Token {
    kind = k,
    span = Span { lo = off, hi = off },
    value = None
  }

fn ly_vopen(off : Int) : Token = ly_virt(TVOpen, off)

fn ly_vclose(off : Int) : Token = ly_virt(TVClose, off)

fn ly_vsep(off : Int) : Token = ly_virt(TVSemi, off)

-- Membership in a list of fixed-token spellings.
fn ly_mem(s : String, xs : List(String)) : Bool =
  match xs of
    Nil => false
    Cons(h, t) => s == h || ly_mem(s, t)

-- The fixed tokens that open a layout block: their following indented line is
-- the block. Matches the compiler's `opens_block` set (the synthetic head opener
-- is handled separately as `LHead`).
fn ly_opener_words() : List(String) =
  [
      "=",
      "then",
      "else",
      "=>",
      "of",
      "with",
      "handler",
      "fn",
      "try",
      "catch",
      "transact",
      "do",
      "where",
      "loop",
    ]

fn ly_opens_block(k : TokenKind) : Bool =
  match k of
    TFixed(s) => ly_mem(s, ly_opener_words())
    _ => false

-- Whether a fixed token opens a bracket group that suppresses layout.
fn ly_is_bopen(k : TokenKind) : Bool =
  match k of
    TFixed(s) => s == "(" || s == "[" || s == "\{"
    _ => false

-- Whether a fixed token closes a bracket group.
fn ly_is_bclose(k : TokenKind) : Bool =
  match k of
    TFixed(s) => s == ")" || s == "]" || s == "\}"
    _ => false

-- Whether a fixed token keeps its opener status across an immediately following
-- bracket group on the same line: `fn`, giving trailing-block-argument syntax.
fn ly_is_carry(k : TokenKind) : Bool =
  match k of
    TFixed(s) => s == "fn"
    _ => false

-- Whether a fixed token is a declaration head whose body is a bare-indent block.
fn ly_opens_decl(k : TokenKind) : Bool =
  match k of
    TFixed(s) => s == "class" || s == "instance" || s == "effect"
    _ => false

-- The start offset of an entry.
fn ly_e_lo(e : LEntry) : Int =
  match e of
    LTok(t) => t.span.lo
    LHead(o) => o

-- The end offset of an entry.
fn ly_e_hi(e : LEntry) : Int =
  match e of
    LTok(t) => t.span.hi
    LHead(o) => o

-- Whether the entry opens a block: a real opener, or a head opener.
fn ly_e_opener(e : LEntry) : Bool =
  match e of
    LTok(t) => ly_opens_block(t.kind)
    LHead(_) => true

fn ly_e_bopen(e : LEntry) : Bool =
  match e of
    LTok(t) => ly_is_bopen(t.kind)
    LHead(_) => false

fn ly_e_bclose(e : LEntry) : Bool =
  match e of
    LTok(t) => ly_is_bclose(t.kind)
    LHead(_) => false

fn ly_e_carry(e : LEntry) : Bool =
  match e of
    LTok(t) => ly_is_carry(t.kind)
    LHead(_) => false

-- Whether text[lo, hi) contains a newline.
fn ly_has_nl(text : String, lo : Int, hi : Int) : Bool =
  if lo >= hi then
    false
  elif byte_at(text, lo) == 10 then
    true
  else
    ly_has_nl(text, lo + 1, hi)

-- Whether two adjacent tokens stay on one line.
fn ly_same_line(text : String, prev_hi : Int, next_lo : Int) : Bool =
  if ly_has_nl(text, prev_hi, next_lo) then
    false
  else
    true

-- Splice a synthetic head opener after each declaration head. The head runs to
-- the last token sharing the keyword's line; the opener is a zero-width entry at
-- the head's end. In brace form the `{` is the head's last token, so the opener
-- lands inside the bracket group where the driver ignores it.
fn ly_inject(text : String, toks : List(Token)) : List(LEntry) =
  reverse(ly_inject_go(text, toks, Nil))

fn ly_inject_go(
  text : String,
  toks : List(Token),
  acc : List(LEntry)
) : List(LEntry) =
  match toks of
    Nil => acc
    Cons(t, rest) =>
      if ly_opens_decl(t.kind) then
        match ly_head_run(text, rest, t.span.hi, Cons(LTok(t), acc)) of
          HeadR { rest = rest2, endoff = endoff, acc = acc2 } =>
            ly_inject_go(text, rest2, Cons(LHead(endoff), acc2))
      else
        ly_inject_go(text, rest, Cons(LTok(t), acc))

fn ly_head_run(
  text : String,
  toks : List(Token),
  endoff : Int,
  acc : List(LEntry)
) : HeadR =
  match toks of
    Nil => HeadR { rest = Nil, endoff = endoff, acc = acc }
    Cons(t, rest) =>
      if ly_same_line(text, endoff, t.span.lo) then
        ly_head_run(text, rest, t.span.hi, Cons(LTok(t), acc))
      else
        HeadR { rest = toks, endoff = endoff, acc = acc }

-- The indent-stack action at column `col`: pop a deeper frame above the floor,
-- separate a sibling at the same column, else nothing. The floor frames are
-- never popped by a line break (Eager keeps the top-level block open).
fn ly_stack_step(stack : List(Int), col : Int, floor : Int) : Close3 =
  match ly_top(stack) of
    None => CNone
    Some(top) =>
      if top > col && ly_depth(stack) > floor then
        CPop
      elif top == col then
        CSep
      else
        CNone

-- Collapse the stack down to `col`, emitting a virtual close per popped frame
-- (anchored at the previous token's end) and a virtual separator for a sibling.
fn ly_close_loop(
  stack : List(Int),
  col : Int,
  last_hi : Int,
  out : List(Token)
) : CloseR =
  match ly_stack_step(stack, col, 1) of
    CPop =>
      ly_close_loop(ly_pop(stack), col, last_hi, Cons(ly_vclose(last_hi), out))
    CSep => CloseR { stack = stack, out = Cons(ly_vsep(last_hi), out) }
    CNone => CloseR { stack = stack, out = out }

-- Whether this token begins a fresh line relative to the previous token.
fn ly_is_newline(prev : Option(Int), cur : Int) : Bool =
  match prev of
    None => true
    Some(pl) => cur > pl

-- Whether no token has been seen yet (the Eager top-level block is still unopen).
fn ly_first(prev : Option(Int)) : Bool =
  match prev of
    None => true
    Some(_) => false

-- The virtual-emission phase: while not inside brackets, open a block for a
-- pending opener that begins a deeper new line (or the very first token), else
-- collapse the stack at a new line; then recompute the opener and carry flags.
-- Inside brackets nothing is emitted and both flags are preserved.
fn ly_phase1(
  e : LEntry,
  st : LState,
  lo : Int,
  col : Int,
  new_line : Bool,
  in_brackets : Bool,
  bopen : Bool,
  out : List(Token)
) : Ph1R =
  if in_brackets then
    Ph1R {
      stack = st.stack,
      out = out,
      po = st.pending_opener,
      carry = st.carrying
    }
  else
    let top_deeper =
      match ly_top(st.stack) of
        None => true
        Some(t) => col > t
    let opens = st.pending_opener && new_line && top_deeper
    let po1 = ly_e_opener(e)
    let carry1 = ly_e_carry(e) || st.carrying && ly_not(new_line) && bopen
    if opens || ly_first(st.prev_line) then
      Ph1R {
        stack = Cons(col, st.stack),
        out = Cons(ly_vopen(lo), out),
        po = po1,
        carry = carry1
      }
    elif new_line then
      match ly_close_loop(st.stack, col, st.last_hi, out) of
        CloseR { stack = stack2, out = out2 } =>
          Ph1R { stack = stack2, out = out2, po = po1, carry = carry1 }
    else
      Ph1R { stack = st.stack, out = out, po = po1, carry = carry1 }

-- Boolean negation, spelled locally to keep call sites terse.
fn ly_not(b : Bool) : Bool =
  if b then
    false
  else
    true

-- The bracket-depth phase: a bracket open deepens the group; a bracket close
-- shallows it and, when the outermost group closes while a carried opener is
-- live, re-arms the pending opener so a following indented line opens a block.
fn ly_phase2(
  bopen : Bool,
  bclose : Bool,
  depth : Int,
  po : Bool,
  carry : Bool
) : Ph2R =
  if bopen then
    Ph2R { depth = depth + 1, po = po, carry = carry }
  elif bclose then
    let d2 =
      if depth > 0 then
        depth - 1
      else
        0
    if d2 == 0 && carry then
      Ph2R { depth = d2, po = true, carry = false }
    else
      Ph2R { depth = d2, po = po, carry = carry }
  else
    Ph2R { depth = depth, po = po, carry = carry }

-- One driver step over an entry: run the virtual-emission and bracket phases,
-- emit the real token (a head opener is dropped), and advance the previous-line
-- and previous-end bookkeeping.
fn ly_step(text : String, e : LEntry, st : LState, out : List(Token)) : StepR =
  let lo = ly_e_lo(e)
  let hi = ly_e_hi(e)
  let col = ly_col(text, lo)
  let cur_line = ly_prev_line(st) + ly_count_nl(text, st.prev_off, lo)
  let new_line = ly_is_newline(st.prev_line, cur_line)
  let in_brackets = st.bracket_depth > 0
  let bopen = ly_e_bopen(e)
  let bclose = ly_e_bclose(e)
  match ly_phase1(e, st, lo, col, new_line, in_brackets, bopen, out) of
    Ph1R { stack = stack1, out = out1, po = po1, carry = carry1 } =>
      match ly_phase2(bopen, bclose, st.bracket_depth, po1, carry1) of
        Ph2R { depth = depth2, po = po2, carry = carry2 } =>
          let out3 =
            match e of
              LHead(_) => out1
              LTok(t) => Cons(t, out1)
          let ploff =
            if hi > lo then
              hi - 1
            else
              lo
          let st2 =
            LState {
              stack = stack1,
              pending_opener = po2,
              carrying = carry2,
              bracket_depth = depth2,
              prev_line = Some(cur_line + ly_count_nl(text, lo, ploff)),
              prev_off = ploff,
              last_hi = hi
            }
          StepR(st2, out3)

-- Close every open block at end of input, emitting a virtual close per frame.
fn ly_drain(stack : List(Int), last_hi : Int, out : List(Token)) : List(Token) =
  match stack of
    Nil => reverse(out)
    Cons(_, rest) => ly_drain(rest, last_hi, Cons(ly_vclose(last_hi), out))

fn ly_run(
  text : String,
  entries : List(LEntry),
  st : LState,
  out : List(Token)
) : List(Token) =
  match entries of
    Nil => ly_drain(st.stack, st.last_hi, out)
    Cons(e, rest) =>
      match ly_step(text, e, st, out) of
        StepR(st2, out2) => ly_run(text, rest, st2, out2)

-- Run the offside driver over the injected entries from a clean initial state.
fn ly_layout(text : String, toks : List(Token)) : List(Token) =
  let entries = ly_inject(text, toks)
  let st0 =
    LState {
      stack = Nil,
      pending_opener = false,
      carrying = false,
      bracket_depth = 0,
      prev_line = None,
      prev_off = 0,
      last_hi = 0
    }
  ly_run(text, entries, st0, Nil)

-- | Tokenize and lay out `text`, reproducing the compiler's post-layout `parse`
-- stream: the raw tokens with the virtual block delimiters spliced in and the
-- synthetic head openers stripped. A lexing failure is propagated unchanged.
pub fn layout(text : String) : Result(List(Token), LexError) =
  match lex_raw(text) of
    Err(e) => Err(e)
    Ok(r) => Ok(ly_layout(text, r.tokens))
