-- | The checked mobility boundary for portable, single-use computations.
--
-- `teleport` runs such a computation as a unit that is safe to move to a fresh
-- runtime. The closure handed to it must capture only content-addressed code and
-- portable data (`@ portable`) and be invoked at most once (`@ once`); the
-- compiler proves that contract at every call site. Running a teleported closure
-- is observationally identical to calling it directly -- how a computation is
-- placed is never observable, the same invariant that makes tier and backend
-- choice invisible -- so `teleport` is the checked boundary, not a change in
-- behavior. Compose it with `Replay.record` for a durable, replayable mobile run.

-- | Run a portable, single-use closure as a mobile unit.
--
-- A closure over top-level code and scalar arguments satisfies the contract,
-- and running it through `teleport` is indistinguishable from calling it:
--
-- ```prism
-- teleport(\() -> 6 * 7)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 42
-- ```
--
-- Capturing a local binding is refused at compile time: a local does not
-- travel, so the closure could not move to a fresh runtime:
--
-- ```prism,compile_fail
-- let n = 6
-- teleport(\() -> n * 7)
-- ```
pub fn teleport(f : (() -> a) @ {once, portable}) : a = f()

Per-type value generators for property testing.

A generator is the unwrapped `Quickcheck.Gen`: a size-bounded draw from the ambient `Random` capability. That makes a run deterministic under a seed (the `Quickcheck` runner serves `Random` from a seeded SplitMix64 stream), and lets a derived instance recurse through its fields' `arbitrary` while composing cleanly with the `Gen` combinators. The primitive instances delegate to `Quickcheck`'s canonical generators, so a derived type draws from the same distributions the hand-written harness does.

Wrap an instance back into a `Gen` with `arb_gen` to feed it to `quickcheck`.

-- | Per-type value generators for property testing.
--
-- A generator is the unwrapped `Quickcheck.Gen`: a size-bounded draw from the
-- ambient `Random` capability. That makes a run deterministic under a seed (the
-- `Quickcheck` runner serves `Random` from a seeded SplitMix64 stream), and lets
-- a derived instance recurse through its fields' `arbitrary` while composing
-- cleanly with the `Gen` combinators. The primitive instances delegate to
-- `Quickcheck`'s canonical generators, so a derived type draws from the same
-- distributions the hand-written harness does.
--
-- Wrap an instance back into a `Gen` with `arb_gen` to feed it to `quickcheck`.

import Quickcheck (..)

-- | A structural generator, sized by a fuel budget. `deriving (Arbitrary)` spends
-- the budget on depth: at each recursive constructor it draws its fields a size
-- smaller, and once the budget runs out it restricts to non-recursive
-- constructors, so generation always terminates.
pub class Arbitrary(a)
  arbitrary : (Int) -> a ! {Random | e}

-- | The generator of an `Arbitrary` type, as a `Quickcheck.Gen` ready for
-- `quickcheck`/`gen_at`.
--
-- ```prism,no_run
-- # import Quickcheck (..)
-- fn prop(xs : List(Int)) : Bool = reverse(reverse(xs)) == xs
--
-- fn main() = println(passed(quickcheck(arb_gen(), prop)))
-- ```
pub fn arb_gen() : Gen(a) given Arbitrary(a) = Gen(\(size) -> arbitrary(size))

instance arbitraryInt : Arbitrary(Int)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_int, size)

instance arbitraryI64 : Arbitrary(I64)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_i64, size)

instance arbitraryU64 : Arbitrary(U64)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_u64, size)

instance arbitraryBool : Arbitrary(Bool)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_bool, size)

instance arbitraryUnit : Arbitrary(Unit)
  fn arbitrary(_size) = ()

instance arbitraryChar : Arbitrary(Char)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_char, size)

instance arbitraryFloat : Arbitrary(Float)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_float, size)

instance arbitraryString : Arbitrary(String)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_string, size)

instance arbitraryOption : Arbitrary(Option(a)) given Arbitrary(a)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_option(Gen(\(s) -> arbitrary(s))), size)

instance arbitraryList : Arbitrary(List(a)) given Arbitrary(a)
  fn arbitrary(size) = gen_run(gen_list(Gen(\(s) -> arbitrary(s))), size)

Time: instants, wall-clock timestamps, durations, and RFC 3339.

Three value types keep the two kinds of clock reading from being confused:

- `Instant` is a monotonic reading (nanoseconds from an unspecified origin). Only differences of instants are meaningful; the origin is arbitrary. Use it to measure elapsed time, never to name a point in the calendar. - `Wall` is a system-clock reading: nanoseconds since the Unix epoch (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z), in UTC. Use it to stamp and format a moment. - `Duration` is a signed span of nanoseconds, the difference of two readings.

Both readings come from the one `Clock` capability (declared in `Concurrent`): `mono_clock` performs `mono_now`, `wall_clock` performs `wall_now`. Which reading a program actually gets is a property of the installed handler, not of the call site. `Concurrent.run_clock` serves every `Clock` op from a virtual counter, so a test's time is a pure function of its `sleep`s; `run_clock_real` here serves the two real reads from the OS clock. Both real reads are recorded capability observations, so a time-reading program replays byte-for-byte.

RFC 3339 formatting and parsing are pure, total, UTC-only string code: no locale, no time zone database (tzdb is a political data blob and belongs in a content-addressed package, not a frozen Std). Timestamps at or after the epoch (non-negative wall readings) are supported.
modules.source:
-- | Time: instants, wall-clock timestamps, durations, and RFC 3339.
--
-- Three value types keep the two kinds of clock reading from being confused:
--
--   - `Instant` is a monotonic reading (nanoseconds from an unspecified origin).
--     Only differences of instants are meaningful; the origin is arbitrary. Use
--     it to measure elapsed time, never to name a point in the calendar.
--   - `Wall` is a system-clock reading: nanoseconds since the Unix epoch
--     (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z), in UTC. Use it to stamp and format a moment.
--   - `Duration` is a signed span of nanoseconds, the difference of two readings.
--
-- Both readings come from the one `Clock` capability (declared in `Concurrent`):
-- `mono_clock` performs `mono_now`, `wall_clock` performs `wall_now`. Which
-- reading a program actually gets is a property of the installed handler, not of
-- the call site. `Concurrent.run_clock` serves every `Clock` op from a virtual
-- counter, so a test's time is a pure function of its `sleep`s; `run_clock_real`
-- here serves the two real reads from the OS clock. Both real reads are recorded
-- capability observations, so a time-reading program replays byte-for-byte.
--
-- RFC 3339 formatting and parsing are pure, total, UTC-only string code: no
-- locale, no time zone database (tzdb is a political data blob and belongs in a
-- content-addressed package, not a frozen Std). Timestamps at or after the epoch
-- (non-negative wall readings) are supported.

import Data.List (..)

import Data.Maybe (..)

import Data.String (..)

import Data.Char (is_digit)

import Concurrent (..)

-- Unit conversions, pinned. A `Duration` is nanoseconds; these name the scale
-- factors so no bare `1000000000` appears at a use site.

-- | Nanoseconds in one second (the `Duration` scale factor for `seconds`).
--
-- ```prism
-- nanos_per_sec()
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1000000000
-- ```
pub fn nanos_per_sec() : Int = 1000000000

-- | Nanoseconds in one millisecond.
pub fn nanos_per_milli() : Int = 1000000

-- | Nanoseconds in one microsecond.
pub fn nanos_per_micro() : Int = 1000

fn secs_per_day() : Int = 86400

fn secs_per_hour() : Int = 3600

fn secs_per_min() : Int = 60

-- | A signed span of time, in nanoseconds.
pub type Duration = Duration(Int)

-- | The span in whole nanoseconds.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(seconds(2))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 2000000000
-- ```
pub fn dur_nanos(d : Duration) : Int =
  match d of
    Duration(n) => n

-- | A duration of `n` nanoseconds.
pub fn nanos(n : Int) : Duration = Duration(n)

-- | A duration of `n` microseconds.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(micros(3))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 3000
-- ```
pub fn micros(n : Int) : Duration = Duration(n * nanos_per_micro())

-- | A duration of `n` milliseconds.
pub fn millis(n : Int) : Duration = Duration(n * nanos_per_milli())

-- | A duration of `n` seconds.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(seconds(1))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1000000000
-- ```
pub fn seconds(n : Int) : Duration = Duration(n * nanos_per_sec())

-- | A duration of `n` minutes.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_as_secs(minutes(2))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 120
-- ```
pub fn minutes(n : Int) : Duration = Duration(n * nanos_per_sec() * secs_per_min())

-- | A duration of `n` hours.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_as_secs(hours(1))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 3600
-- ```
pub fn hours(n : Int) : Duration = Duration(n * nanos_per_sec() * secs_per_hour())

-- | The whole-second part of a duration (truncated toward zero).
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_as_secs(dur_add(seconds(90), millis(500)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 90
-- ```
pub fn dur_as_secs(d : Duration) : Int = dur_nanos(d) / nanos_per_sec()

-- | The whole-millisecond part of a duration (truncated toward zero).
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_as_millis(seconds(2))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 2000
-- ```
pub fn dur_as_millis(d : Duration) : Int = dur_nanos(d) / nanos_per_milli()

-- | Sum of two durations.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(dur_add(seconds(1), millis(500)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1500000000
-- ```
pub fn dur_add(a : Duration, b : Duration) : Duration =
  Duration(dur_nanos(a) + dur_nanos(b))

-- | Difference of two durations (`a - b`).
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(dur_sub(seconds(2), millis(500)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1500000000
-- ```
pub fn dur_sub(a : Duration, b : Duration) : Duration =
  Duration(dur_nanos(a) - dur_nanos(b))

-- | A duration scaled by an integer factor.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(dur_scale(seconds(1), 3))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 3000000000
-- ```
pub fn dur_scale(a : Duration, k : Int) : Duration = Duration(dur_nanos(a) * k)

-- | A duration with the sign flipped.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(dur_negate(seconds(1)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- -1000000000
-- ```
pub fn dur_negate(a : Duration) : Duration = Duration(0 - dur_nanos(a))

-- | Ordering of two durations (`-1`, `0`, `1`).
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_cmp(seconds(1), seconds(2))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- -1
-- ```
pub fn dur_cmp(a : Duration, b : Duration) : Int =
  let x = dur_nanos(a)
  let y = dur_nanos(b)
  if x < y then
    -1
  elif x > y then
    1
  else
    0

-- | True when the two durations are equal.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_eq(millis(1000), seconds(1))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- true
-- ```
pub fn dur_eq(a : Duration, b : Duration) : Bool = dur_cmp(a, b) == 0

-- | A monotonic clock reading, in nanoseconds from an unspecified origin.
pub type Instant = Instant(Int)

-- | The raw monotonic reading in nanoseconds. The absolute value is meaningless
-- across processes; subtract two instants to get an elapsed `Duration`.
--
-- ```prism
-- instant_nanos(Instant(500))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 500
-- ```
pub fn instant_nanos(i : Instant) : Int =
  match i of
    Instant(n) => n

-- | The span from `earlier` to `later` (`later - earlier`). Named `elapsed`, not
-- `between`, to leave Base's numeric `between` range test unshadowed.
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(elapsed(Instant(100), Instant(450)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 350
-- ```
pub fn elapsed(earlier : Instant, later : Instant) : Duration =
  Duration(instant_nanos(later) - instant_nanos(earlier))

-- | An instant advanced by a duration.
--
-- ```prism
-- instant_nanos(instant_add(Instant(100), micros(1)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1100
-- ```
pub fn instant_add(i : Instant, d : Duration) : Instant =
  Instant(instant_nanos(i) + dur_nanos(d))

-- | A wall-clock reading: nanoseconds since the Unix epoch, in UTC.
pub type Wall = Wall(Int)

-- | The reading in nanoseconds since the Unix epoch (UTC).
--
-- ```prism
-- wall_nanos(wall_of_nanos(1500000000))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1500000000
-- ```
pub fn wall_nanos(w : Wall) : Int =
  match w of
    Wall(n) => n

-- | A wall reading from nanoseconds since the Unix epoch.
pub fn wall_of_nanos(n : Int) : Wall = Wall(n)

-- | Whole seconds since the Unix epoch (truncated toward zero).
--
-- ```prism
-- wall_unix_secs(wall_of_nanos(1500000000))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1
-- ```
pub fn wall_unix_secs(w : Wall) : Int = wall_nanos(w) / nanos_per_sec()

-- | A wall reading advanced by a duration.
--
-- ```prism
-- wall_nanos(wall_add(wall_of_nanos(0), seconds(1)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1000000000
-- ```
pub fn wall_add(w : Wall, d : Duration) : Wall = Wall(wall_nanos(w) + dur_nanos(d))

-- | The span from `earlier` to `later` wall readings (`later - earlier`).
--
-- ```prism
-- dur_nanos(wall_diff(wall_of_nanos(0), wall_of_nanos(500)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 500
-- ```
pub fn wall_diff(earlier : Wall, later : Wall) : Duration =
  Duration(wall_nanos(later) - wall_nanos(earlier))

-- | Ordering of two wall readings (`-1`, `0`, `1`).
--
-- ```prism
-- wall_cmp(wall_of_nanos(1), wall_of_nanos(2))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- -1
-- ```
pub fn wall_cmp(a : Wall, b : Wall) : Int =
  let x = wall_nanos(a)
  let y = wall_nanos(b)
  if x < y then
    -1
  elif x > y then
    1
  else
    0

-- | Read the monotonic clock. Deterministic under `run_clock`, real (and
-- recorded) under `run_clock_real`.
--
-- ```prism,no_run
-- run_clock_real(\() -> mono_clock())
-- ```
pub fn mono_clock() : Instant = Instant(mono_now())

-- | Read the wall clock. Deterministic under `run_clock`, real (and recorded)
-- under `run_clock_real`.
--
-- ```prism,no_run
-- format_rfc3339(run_clock_real(\() -> wall_clock()))
-- ```
pub fn wall_clock() : Wall = Wall(wall_now())

-- | Run `action` against the real OS clock. `now`/`sleep` still thread a virtual
-- counter (they are the scheduler's logical time), so this is a superset of
-- `run_clock`: `wall_now` and `mono_now` read the real clock through the `prim_*`
-- builtins, each a recorded observation, and everything else stays virtual.
--
-- ```prism,no_run
-- run_clock_real(\() -> wall_unix_secs(wall_clock()))
-- ```
pub fn run_clock_real(action : () -> a ! {Clock | e}) : a =
  let g =
    handle action() with
      now() resume k => \(t) -> k(t)(t)
      sleep(d) resume k => \(t) -> k(())(t + d)
      wall_now() resume k => \(t) -> k(prim_wall_now())(t)
      mono_now() resume k => \(t) -> k(prim_mono_now())(t)
      return r => \(_t) -> r
  g(0)

-- Civil-calendar conversions (Howard Hinnant's algorithms), valid for the
-- proleptic Gregorian calendar. Every intermediate is non-negative for dates at
-- or after the epoch, so truncating division coincides with floor division.

-- Days since 1970-01-01 for the given civil date.
fn days_from_civil(y : Int, m : Int, d : Int) : Int =
  let yy =
    if m <= 2 then
      y - 1
    else
      y
  let era = yy / 400
  let yoe = yy - era * 400
  let mp =
    if m > 2 then
      m - 3
    else
      m + 9
  let doy = (153 * mp + 2) / 5 + d - 1
  let doe = yoe * 365 + yoe / 4 - yoe / 100 + doy
  era * 146097 + doe - 719468

-- Civil (year, month, day) for a day count since 1970-01-01.
fn civil_from_days(z0 : Int) : (Int, Int, Int) =
  let z = z0 + 719468
  let era = z / 146097
  let doe = z - era * 146097
  let yoe = (doe - doe / 1460 + doe / 36524 - doe / 146096) / 365
  let y = yoe + era * 400
  let doy = doe - (365 * yoe + yoe / 4 - yoe / 100)
  let mp = (5 * doy + 2) / 153
  let d = doy - (153 * mp + 2) / 5 + 1
  let m =
    if mp < 10 then
      mp + 3
    else
      mp - 9
  let year =
    if m <= 2 then
      y + 1
    else
      y
  (year, m, d)

-- Zero-pad the decimal form of a non-negative `n` to at least `w` digits.
fn pad0(n : Int, w : Int) : String =
  let s = show_int(n)
  concat(str_repeat("0", w - str_len(s)), s)

-- | Format a wall reading as an RFC 3339 timestamp in UTC, e.g.
-- `2026-07-04T12:34:56Z`. A nonzero sub-second part is emitted as exactly nine
-- fractional digits (nanoseconds); an exact second emits no fraction. The output
-- is canonical: one reading formats to one string, so timestamps are comparable
-- and hashable as text.
--
-- ```prism
-- format_rfc3339(wall_of_nanos(0))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z
-- ```
pub fn format_rfc3339(w : Wall) : String =
  let ns = wall_nanos(w)
  let secs = ns / nanos_per_sec()
  let sub = ns % nanos_per_sec()
  let days = secs / secs_per_day()
  let tod = secs % secs_per_day()
  let (y, mo, d) = civil_from_days(days)
  let hh = tod / secs_per_hour()
  let mm = tod % secs_per_hour() / secs_per_min()
  let ss = tod % secs_per_min()
  let date = concat(
      pad0(y, 4),
      concat("-", concat(pad0(mo, 2), concat("-", pad0(d, 2)))),
    )
  let time = concat(
      pad0(hh, 2),
      concat(":", concat(pad0(mm, 2), concat(":", pad0(ss, 2)))),
    )
  let frac =
    if sub == 0 then
      ""
    else
      concat(".", pad0(sub, 9))
  concat(date, concat("T", concat(time, concat(frac, "Z"))))

-- Read a fixed-width run of decimal digits at `[i, i+w)` as an Int, or `None` if
-- the field runs off the end or holds a non-digit.
fn digits(s : String, i : Int, w : Int) : Option(Int) =
  if i + w > str_len(s) then
    None
  else
    digits_go(s, i, i + w, 0)

fn digits_go(s : String, i : Int, hi : Int, acc : Int) : Option(Int) =
  if i >= hi then
    Some(acc)
  else
    let c = char_at(s, i)
    if is_digit(c) then
      digits_go(s, i + 1, hi, acc * 10 + c - 48)
    else
      None

-- True when `s` has char `c` at index `i`.
fn char_is(s : String, i : Int, c : Int) : Bool =
  i < str_len(s) && char_at(s, i) == c

-- Parse the optional fractional seconds beginning at `i` (a leading '.'), padding
-- or truncating to nanosecond precision. Returns the nanoseconds and the index
-- just past the fraction.
fn parse_frac(s : String, i : Int) : (Int, Int) =
  if char_is(s, i, 46) then
    frac_go(s, i + 1, 0, 0)
  else
    (0, i)

fn frac_go(s : String, i : Int, seen : Int, acc : Int) : (Int, Int) =
  if i < str_len(s) && is_digit(char_at(s, i)) then
    let acc2 =
      if seen < 9 then
        acc * 10 + char_at(s, i) - 48
      else
        acc
    frac_go(s, i + 1, seen + 1, acc2)
  else
    (scale_frac(acc, min(seen, 9)), i)

-- Scale `acc` (a `d`-digit fraction) up to nine digits (nanoseconds).
fn scale_frac(acc : Int, d : Int) : Int =
  if d >= 9 then
    acc
  else
    scale_frac(acc * 10, d + 1)

-- Parse the trailing zone designator at `i`: `Z`, or `(+|-)HH:MM`. Returns the
-- offset from UTC in seconds (to subtract), or `None` if malformed or if trailing
-- input remains.
fn parse_zone(s : String, i : Int) : Option(Int) =
  if char_is(s, i, 90) && i + 1 == str_len(s) then
    Some(0)
  elif ((char_is(s, i, 43) || char_is(s, i, 45))
      && i + 6 == str_len(s)
      && char_is(s, i + 3, 58)) then
    match (digits(s, i + 1, 2), digits(s, i + 4, 2)) of
      (Some(oh), Some(om)) =>
        let mag = oh * secs_per_hour() + om * secs_per_min()
        if char_is(s, i, 43) then
          Some(mag)
        else
          Some(0 - mag)
      _ => None
  else
    None

-- True when `lo <= x <= hi`.
fn in_range(x : Int, lo : Int, hi : Int) : Bool = x >= lo && x <= hi

-- | Parse an RFC 3339 timestamp to a wall reading in UTC, or `None` if the string
-- is not a well-formed `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.frac](Z|(+|-)HH:MM)`. The date/time
-- separators are checked, field ranges are validated, an offset is folded into
-- UTC, and any trailing input is rejected, so the parser is total: a malformed or
-- overlong string is `None`, never a partial or wrapped value.
--
-- ```prism
-- wall_unix_secs(unwrap_or(wall_of_nanos(0), parse_rfc3339("2000-01-01T00:00:00Z")))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 946684800
-- ```
pub fn parse_rfc3339(s : String) : Option(Wall) =
  if str_len(s) < 20 then
    None
  elif (not(char_is(s, 4, 45) && char_is(s, 7, 45) && char_is(s, 10, 84))) then
    None
  elif not(char_is(s, 13, 58) && char_is(s, 16, 58)) then
    None
  else
    match ((
          digits(s, 0, 4),
          digits(s, 5, 2),
          digits(s, 8, 2),
          digits(s, 11, 2),
          digits(s, 14, 2),
          digits(s, 17, 2),
        )) of
      (Some(y), Some(mo), Some(d), Some(hh), Some(mm), Some(ss)) =>
        if (in_range(mo, 1, 12)
            && in_range(d, 1, 31)
            && in_range(hh, 0, 23)
            && in_range(mm, 0, 59)
            && in_range(ss, 0, 60)) then
          let (sub, j) = parse_frac(s, 19)
          match parse_zone(s, j) of
            Some(offset) =>
              let days = days_from_civil(y, mo, d)
              let secs = days * secs_per_day()
                + hh * secs_per_hour()
                + mm * secs_per_min()
                + ss
                - offset
              Some(Wall(secs * nanos_per_sec() + sub))
            None => None
        else
          None
      _ => None

The opt-in serialization layer.

Serialization is deliberately out of Base: a program that never persists a value imports none of this. Everything here is pure total functions over `Bytes`; writing those bytes to a file, a socket, or a replay log is a capability routed through the effect system, never performed here.

The surface has three layers. The `Serialize` class and its instances are the codec: a value's compact positional body, derived structurally by `deriving (Serialize)` and bottoming out in the primitive instances below. The envelope (`wire_encode_stable`/`wire_decode_stable`, or the explicit-digest `*_with_digest` escape hatches) wraps a body in the frame `[scheme tag][kind][contract digest][body?]`, checked before the body so a stale layout is rejected up front. The version ladder (`compose_upgrade`/ `compose_downgrade`) spans frozen versions with O(n) adjacent converters.

## The frame

Every serialized thing is one envelope, read left to right, each header part checked before the next is touched:

```text
   +------------+------+-----------------+ - - - - - - +
   | scheme tag | kind | contract digest |    body?    |
   +------------+------+-----------------+ - - - - - - +

   scheme tag       length-prefixed string, always "prism-core-hash-v2";
                    a foreign scheme is rejected before anything else
   kind             uvarint naming what the digest identifies:
                    value 0, def 1, protocol 2, kont 3, cert 4
   contract digest  length-prefixed hex shape digest of the expected
                    layout, checked before the body is decoded
   body?            the compact positional encoding below; an absent
                    body is a pure reference, named by its digest

   body encoding    Int and I64 as zigzag LEB128 varints, U64 and
                    constructor tags as plain LEB128, strings and
                    lists length-prefixed with the length bounded on
                    both encode and decode, a sum as its constructor
                    tag followed by its arguments, a product as its
                    fields in declaration order, no padding
```

## The `Bytes` representation

`Bytes` is an unboxed byte buffer (`Buf`, `runtime/prism_buffer.c`) plus a read cursor: `Bytes(buf, off)` is the bytes `buf[off ..]`. The buffer holds raw u8 with no UTF-8 interpretation, so it threads byte-for-byte identically on both backends (the parity contract a `String`-of-bytes would break, since reconstructing a `String` from raw bytes repairs invalid UTF-8 lossily). The cursor makes `decode` cheap: peeling a byte off the front advances the offset in O(1) with no copy, so a whole decode is linear. Encode accumulates into a growable buffer builder (`buf_push`, amortized O(1)), so building a container or a string body stays linear rather than paying the quadratic cost a right-nested immutable `wire_cat` would incur. The concrete representation is owned by the codec; a derived instance only ever threads a `Bytes` through the builders below, never inspects it. `bytes_of_list`/`bytes_to_list` bridge to the older `List(Int)` view for callers that still want it.

## Totality

`decode` is total. Every read consumes at least one byte from a finite, strictly shrinking list, so decode always terminates; a truncated or hostile input runs out of bytes and fails through `Fail` rather than looping or panicking. Varints are length-capped and container and string lengths are bounded on both encode and decode, so a hostile length prefix cannot force unbounded work. The frame's total decoder checks the scheme, kind, and digest before touching the body and rejects trailing bytes after the value.

## Deriving

`deriving (Serialize)` writes the codec: a product encodes its fields in declaration order, a sum prefixes a constructor tag, and each field defers to its own instance. `deriving (Stable)` succeeds only when every component is itself `Stable`, so the derivability is the proof that a frozen format contains no unserializable value.

-- | The opt-in serialization layer.
--
-- Serialization is deliberately out of Base: a program that
-- never persists a value imports none of this. Everything here is pure total
-- functions over `Bytes`; writing those bytes to a file, a socket, or a replay
-- log is a capability routed through the effect system, never performed here.
--
-- The surface has three layers. The `Serialize` class and its instances are the
-- codec: a value's compact positional body, derived structurally by
-- `deriving (Serialize)` and bottoming out in the primitive instances below. The
-- envelope (`wire_encode_stable`/`wire_decode_stable`, or the explicit-digest
-- `*_with_digest` escape hatches) wraps a body in the frame
-- `[scheme tag][kind][contract digest][body?]`, checked before the body so a
-- stale layout is rejected up front. The version ladder (`compose_upgrade`/
-- `compose_downgrade`) spans frozen versions with O(n) adjacent converters.
--
-- ## The frame
--
-- Every serialized thing is one envelope, read left to right, each header part
-- checked before the next is touched:
--
-- ```text
--    +------------+------+-----------------+ - - - - - - +
--    | scheme tag | kind | contract digest |    body?    |
--    +------------+------+-----------------+ - - - - - - +
--
--    scheme tag       length-prefixed string, always "prism-core-hash-v2";
--                     a foreign scheme is rejected before anything else
--    kind             uvarint naming what the digest identifies:
--                     value 0, def 1, protocol 2, kont 3, cert 4
--    contract digest  length-prefixed hex shape digest of the expected
--                     layout, checked before the body is decoded
--    body?            the compact positional encoding below; an absent
--                     body is a pure reference, named by its digest
--
--    body encoding    Int and I64 as zigzag LEB128 varints, U64 and
--                     constructor tags as plain LEB128, strings and
--                     lists length-prefixed with the length bounded on
--                     both encode and decode, a sum as its constructor
--                     tag followed by its arguments, a product as its
--                     fields in declaration order, no padding
-- ```
--
-- ## The `Bytes` representation
--
-- `Bytes` is an unboxed byte buffer (`Buf`, `runtime/prism_buffer.c`) plus a read
-- cursor: `Bytes(buf, off)` is the bytes `buf[off ..]`. The buffer holds raw u8
-- with no UTF-8 interpretation, so it threads byte-for-byte identically on both
-- backends (the parity contract a `String`-of-bytes would break, since
-- reconstructing a `String` from raw bytes repairs invalid UTF-8 lossily). The cursor
-- makes `decode` cheap: peeling a byte off the front advances the offset in O(1)
-- with no copy, so a whole decode is linear. Encode accumulates into a growable
-- buffer builder (`buf_push`, amortized O(1)), so building a container or a
-- string body stays linear rather than paying the quadratic cost a right-nested
-- immutable `wire_cat` would incur. The concrete representation is owned by the
-- codec; a derived instance only ever threads a `Bytes` through the builders
-- below, never inspects it. `bytes_of_list`/`bytes_to_list` bridge to the older
-- `List(Int)` view for callers that still want it.
--
-- ## Totality
--
-- `decode` is total. Every read consumes at least one byte from a finite,
-- strictly shrinking list, so decode always terminates; a truncated or hostile
-- input runs out of bytes and fails through `Fail` rather than looping or
-- panicking. Varints are length-capped and container and string lengths are
-- bounded on both encode and decode, so a hostile length prefix cannot force
-- unbounded work. The frame's total decoder checks the scheme, kind, and digest
-- before touching the body and rejects trailing bytes after the value.
--
-- ## Deriving
--
-- `deriving (Serialize)` writes the codec: a product encodes its fields in
-- declaration order, a sum prefixes a constructor tag, and each field defers to
-- its own instance. `deriving (Stable)` succeeds only when every component is
-- itself `Stable`, so the derivability is the proof that a frozen format contains
-- no unserializable value.

import Data.List (..)

import Data.Foldable (..)

import Data.Map (..)

-- The varint radix (7 data bits per byte, the eighth a continuation flag) and the
-- byte cap that bounds a single varint, so a hostile all-continuation run cannot
-- read forever. Ten radix-128 groups cover a full 64-bit magnitude.
let varint_radix : Int = 128

let varint_max_bytes : Int = 10

-- The inclusive length bound on a decoded string or container, enforced on encode
-- and decode alike so a hostile length prefix is rejected outright (2^20 bytes).
let wire_len_max : Int = 1048576

-- The largest Unicode scalar a `Char` may decode to (U+10FFFF).
let char_max : Int = 1114111

-- A byte value is masked into `0..255` on the way in, so a builder never smuggles
-- a wider word into the buffer.
let byte_mask : Int = 256

-- | A compact, positional byte body: an unboxed byte buffer and a read cursor,
-- `Bytes(buf, off)` denoting the bytes `buf[off ..]`. The concrete representation
-- is owned by the codec; a derived instance only ever threads a `Bytes` through
-- the builders below, never inspects it.
pub type Bytes = Bytes(Buf, Int)

-- | What a downgrade could not carry down: the names of the fields dropped when
-- lowering a value to an older frozen version. A downgrade never silently
-- discards, it reports every field it had to drop.
pub type Loss = Loss(List(String))

-- | The codec, derived structurally by `deriving (Serialize)`. `encode` writes a
-- value's compact positional body; `decode` reads one back, returning the value
-- alongside the bytes that follow it so a reader can thread a frame's fields in
-- declaration order. Decode is total: it fails through `Fail` on a truncated or
-- malformed body rather than panicking, so hostile input is one ordinary failure
-- channel.
--
-- `decode(encode(x))` recovers the value (and the bytes that followed it):
--
-- ```prism
-- (fst(decode(encode(42))) : Int)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 42
-- ```
pub class Serialize(a)
  encode : (a) -> Bytes
  decode : (Bytes) -> (a, Bytes) ! {Fail | e}

-- | The structural witness that a type's format is frozen-serializable: a record
-- is `Stable` when all its fields are, a sum when all its variants' arguments are.
-- The derivability is the whole content of the proof: persisting a type with a
-- non-stable component (a function, an effectful thunk) fails at the `deriving
-- (Stable)` site, at compile time, naming the offending field.
--
-- The one method, `shape_digest_of`, is the type's contract digest: the shape
-- digest of its frozen layout. A derived instance's body is that digest injected by
-- the compiler from its single shape-digest computation, so `shape_digest_of` is a
-- per-type constant no source can forge (`Stable` is derive-only; a hand-written
-- instance is rejected). The argument is used only to resolve the instance by
-- value; the digest does not depend on it. `wire_encode_stable`/`wire_decode_stable`
-- read it, so ordinary code never hand-threads a digest string into the envelope.
pub class Stable(a)
  shape_digest_of : (a) -> String

-- Wrap a whole buffer (cursor at 0) as a body, and recover the buffer of a body's
-- remaining bytes (compacting away a non-zero cursor with a single slice). The
-- representation seam between the buffer and the `Bytes` view; `Data.Bytes` builds
-- its utility layer over these three, never the `Bytes` constructor directly.
-- | Wrap a whole buffer (cursor at 0) as a byte body.
--
-- ```prism
-- wire_len(bytes_of_buf(buf_empty()))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 0
-- ```
pub fn bytes_of_buf(b : Buf) : Bytes = Bytes(b, 0)

-- | Recover the buffer of a body's remaining bytes, compacting away a non-zero
-- cursor with a single slice.
pub fn bytes_buf(bs : Bytes) : Buf =
  match bs of
    Bytes(b, off) =>
      if off == 0 then
        b
      else
        buf_slice(b, off, buf_len(b) - off)

-- | The i-th byte of a body, from the cursor. Bounds are the caller's contract
-- (the readers check emptiness first); an out-of-range index traps.
--
-- ```prism
-- bytes_at(bytes_of_list([10, 20, 30]), 1)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 20
-- ```
pub fn bytes_at(bs : Bytes, i : Int) : Int =
  match bs of
    Bytes(b, off) => buf_get(b, off + i)

-- The empty body.
pub let wire_empty : Bytes = Bytes(buf_empty(), 0)

-- | Concatenate two byte bodies into a fresh buffer.
--
-- ```prism
-- bytes_to_list(wire_cat(bytes_of_list([1, 2]), bytes_of_list([3])))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- [1, 2, 3]
-- ```
pub fn wire_cat(a : Bytes, b : Bytes) : Bytes =
  bytes_of_buf(buf_cat(bytes_buf(a), bytes_buf(b)))

-- A one-byte body, the value masked into `0..255`.
fn wire_byte(b : Int) : Bytes =
  bytes_of_buf(buf_push(buf_empty(), mod(b, byte_mask)))

-- Peel one byte off the front, or `fail()` when the body is exhausted. This is
-- the single place a truncated input turns into a `Fail`. Advancing the cursor is
-- O(1) and copy-free.
fn wire_uncons(bs : Bytes) : (Int, Bytes) =
  if wire_is_empty(bs) then
    fail()
  else
    match bs of
      Bytes(b, off) => (buf_get(b, off), Bytes(b, off + 1))

-- | True when a body has no bytes left. The reader uses it to reject trailing
-- bytes after a value, and a peer uses it to tell a reference frame (no body)
-- from an inline one.
--
-- ```prism
-- wire_is_empty(wire_empty)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- true
-- ```
pub fn wire_is_empty(bs : Bytes) : Bool = wire_len(bs) == 0

-- | The number of bytes in a body.
--
-- ```prism
-- wire_len(bytes_of_list([1, 2, 3]))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 3
-- ```
pub fn wire_len(bs : Bytes) : Int =
  match bs of
    Bytes(b, off) => buf_len(b) - off

-- Append every byte of a body onto a growable buffer, the linear accumulation
-- primitive the encoders fold through instead of a right-nested `wire_cat`.
fn buf_append(acc : Buf, bs : Bytes) : Buf =
  match bs of
    Bytes(b, off) => buf_append_go(acc, b, off, buf_len(b))

fn buf_append_go(acc : Buf, b : Buf, i : Int, n : Int) : Buf =
  if i >= n then
    acc
  else
    buf_append_go(buf_push(acc, buf_get(b, i)), b, i + 1, n)

-- | Build a body from a `List(Int)` of byte values (each masked into `0..255`),
-- and read a body back out as that list. These bridge the buffer representation
-- to the older list view for callers that thread bytes as ordinary data.
--
-- ```prism
-- bytes_to_list(bytes_of_list([1, 2, 3]))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- [1, 2, 3]
-- ```
pub fn bytes_of_list(xs : List(Int)) : Bytes =
  bytes_of_buf(list_to_buf(buf_empty(), xs))

fn list_to_buf(acc : Buf, xs : List(Int)) : Buf =
  match xs of
    Nil => acc
    Cons(h, t) => list_to_buf(buf_push(acc, mod(h, byte_mask)), t)

pub fn bytes_to_list(bs : Bytes) : List(Int) = bytes_to_list_go(bs, 0, wire_len(bs))

fn bytes_to_list_go(bs : Bytes, i : Int, n : Int) : List(Int) =
  if i >= n then
    Nil
  else
    Cons(bytes_at(bs, i), bytes_to_list_go(bs, i + 1, n))

-- An unsigned LEB128 varint: the low seven bits per byte, the high bit set on
-- every byte but the last. Small values cost one byte.
fn put_uvarint(n : Int) : Bytes =
  let lo = mod(n, varint_radix)
  let hi = n / varint_radix
  if hi == 0 then
    wire_byte(lo)
  else
    wire_cat(wire_byte(lo + varint_radix), put_uvarint(hi))

-- Read an unsigned varint low-to-high, capped at `varint_max_bytes` so a hostile
-- run of continuation bytes cannot read unboundedly. `mult` is the place value of
-- the current group.
fn get_uvarint_go(
  bs : Bytes,
  mult : Int,
  acc : Int,
  count : Int
) : (Int, Bytes) =
  if count >= varint_max_bytes then
    fail()
  else
    match wire_uncons(bs) of
      (b, rest) =>
        let acc2 = acc + mod(b, varint_radix) * mult
        if b < varint_radix then
          (acc2, rest)
        else
          get_uvarint_go(rest, mult * varint_radix, acc2, count + 1)

fn get_uvarint(bs : Bytes) : (Int, Bytes) = get_uvarint_go(bs, 1, 0, 0)

-- | Encode a constructor tag (a small non-negative integer) as a varint. The
-- derived `Serialize` for a sum prefixes its body with this.
--
-- ```prism
-- bytes_to_list(wire_tag(300))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- [172, 2]
-- ```
pub fn wire_tag(i : Int) : Bytes = put_uvarint(i)

-- | Peel a constructor tag off the front of a body, returning it and the rest.
-- The derived `Serialize` for a sum reads this before dispatching on the tag.
--
-- ```prism
-- fst(wire_get_tag(wire_tag(300)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 300
-- ```
pub fn wire_get_tag(bs : Bytes) : (Int, Bytes) = get_uvarint(bs)

-- Zigzag a signed integer to a non-negative one so small negatives stay small
-- under LEB128: `0, -1, 1, -2, 2 -> 0, 1, 2, 3, 4`.
fn zigzag(x : Int) : Int =
  if x >= 0 then
    2 * x
  else
    -1 - 2 * x

fn unzigzag(z : Int) : Int =
  if mod(z, 2) == 0 then
    z / 2
  else
    (-1 - z) / 2

fn put_svarint(x : Int) : Bytes = put_uvarint(zigzag(x))

fn get_svarint(bs : Bytes) : (Int, Bytes) =
  match get_uvarint(bs) of
    (z, r) => (unzigzag(z), r)

instance serializeInt : Serialize(Int)
  fn encode(x) = put_svarint(x)
  fn decode(bs) = get_svarint(bs)

-- The primitive and container codecs. Each instance method is a one-liner that
-- delegates to a top-level `enc_*`/`dec_*` function, so the readers that thread
-- and pattern-match the remaining bytes stay ordinary functions.
fn dec_i64(bs : Bytes) : (I64, Bytes) =
  match get_svarint(bs) of
    (n, r) => (to_i64(n), r)

instance serializeI64 : Serialize(I64)
  fn encode(x) = put_svarint(int_of_i64(x))
  fn decode(bs) = dec_i64(bs)

fn dec_u64(bs : Bytes) : (U64, Bytes) =
  match get_uvarint(bs) of
    (n, r) => (to_u64(n), r)

instance serializeU64 : Serialize(U64)
  fn encode(x) = put_uvarint(int_of_u64(x))
  fn decode(bs) = dec_u64(bs)

fn enc_bool(b : Bool) : Bytes = wire_byte(if b then 1 else 0)

fn dec_bool(bs : Bytes) : (Bool, Bytes) =
  match wire_uncons(bs) of
    (v, r) =>
      if v == 0 then
        (false, r)
      elif v == 1 then
        (true, r)
      else
        fail()

instance serializeBool : Serialize(Bool)
  fn encode(b) = enc_bool(b)
  fn decode(bs) = dec_bool(bs)

instance serializeUnit : Serialize(Unit)
  fn encode(_u) = wire_empty
  fn decode(bs) = ((), bs)

fn dec_char(bs : Bytes) : (Char, Bytes) =
  match get_uvarint(bs) of
    (n, r) =>
      if n > char_max then
        fail()
      else
        (chr(n), r)

instance serializeChar : Serialize(Char)
  fn encode(c) = put_uvarint(ord(c))
  fn decode(bs) = dec_char(bs)

-- Append a string's raw UTF-8 bytes to a body, one byte per index, accumulated
-- left-to-right into a buffer builder so the whole body is one linear pass. A
-- `String` is always valid UTF-8, so reconstructing it with `string_of_buf` on
-- decode is lossless on both backends.
fn string_body(s : String, i : Int, n : Int) : Bytes =
  bytes_of_buf(string_body_go(buf_empty(), s, i, n))

fn string_body_go(acc : Buf, s : String, i : Int, n : Int) : Buf =
  if i >= n then
    acc
  else
    string_body_go(buf_push(acc, byte_at(s, i)), s, i + 1, n)

-- Read exactly `n` bytes into a buffer builder, failing if the body runs out
-- first. Accumulated left-to-right so the whole read is one linear pass.
fn take_bytes(bs : Bytes, n : Int, acc : Buf) : (Buf, Bytes) =
  if n <= 0 then
    (acc, bs)
  else
    match wire_uncons(bs) of
      (b, rest) => take_bytes(rest, n - 1, buf_push(acc, b))

fn enc_string(s : String) : Bytes =
  wire_cat(put_uvarint(byte_len(s)), string_body(s, 0, byte_len(s)))

fn dec_string(bs : Bytes) : (String, Bytes) =
  match get_uvarint(bs) of
    (n, r) =>
      if n > wire_len_max then
        fail()
      else
        match take_bytes(r, n, buf_empty()) of
          (buf, rest) => (string_of_buf(buf), rest)

instance serializeString : Serialize(String)
  fn encode(s) = enc_string(s)
  fn decode(bs) = dec_string(bs)

-- Encode a list's elements in order, no per-element framing (the length prefix
-- fixes the count). Accumulated into a buffer builder so the whole encode is one
-- linear pass rather than a chain of copying concatenations.
fn encode_elems(xs : List(a)) : Bytes given Serialize(a) =
  bytes_of_buf(encode_elems_go(buf_empty(), xs))

fn encode_elems_go(acc : Buf, xs : List(a)) : Buf given Serialize(a) =
  match xs of
    Nil => acc
    Cons(h, t) => encode_elems_go(buf_append(acc, encode(h)), t)

-- Decode exactly `n` elements, threading the remaining bytes. Each element read
-- consumes at least one byte, so a hostile length is bounded by the input.
fn decode_elems(bs : Bytes, n : Int) : (List(a), Bytes) given Serialize(a) =
  if n <= 0 then
    (Nil, bs)
  else
    match decode(bs) of
      (x, r1) =>
        match decode_elems(r1, n - 1) of
          (xs, r2) => (Cons(x, xs), r2)

fn enc_list(xs : List(a)) : Bytes given Serialize(a) =
  wire_cat(put_uvarint(length(xs)), encode_elems(xs))

fn dec_list(bs : Bytes) : (List(a), Bytes) given Serialize(a) =
  match get_uvarint(bs) of
    (n, r) =>
      if n > wire_len_max then
        fail()
      else
        decode_elems(r, n)

instance serializeList : Serialize(List(a)) given Serialize(a)
  fn encode(xs) = enc_list(xs)
  fn decode(bs) = dec_list(bs)

-- `Bytes` is itself serializable as its length followed by one signed varint per
-- byte value (the `Serialize(Int)` element codec), so a body may carry another
-- already-encoded body verbatim (the incremental snapshot stores each memo's
-- result bytes this way). This is the same frozen format the older `List(Int)`
-- representation produced (`enc_list` over the byte list); only the storage under
-- it changed, so the bytes on the wire are byte-for-byte identical.
fn enc_bytes(b : Bytes) : Bytes =
  wire_cat(put_uvarint(wire_len(b)), enc_bytes_body(b))

fn enc_bytes_body(b : Bytes) : Bytes =
  bytes_of_buf(enc_bytes_go(buf_empty(), b, 0, wire_len(b)))

fn enc_bytes_go(acc : Buf, b : Bytes, i : Int, n : Int) : Buf =
  if i >= n then
    acc
  else
    enc_bytes_go(buf_append(acc, put_svarint(bytes_at(b, i))), b, i + 1, n)

fn dec_bytes(bs : Bytes) : (Bytes, Bytes) =
  match get_uvarint(bs) of
    (n, r) =>
      if n > wire_len_max then
        fail()
      else
        dec_bytes_go(buf_empty(), r, n)

fn dec_bytes_go(acc : Buf, bs : Bytes, n : Int) : (Bytes, Bytes) =
  if n <= 0 then
    (bytes_of_buf(acc), bs)
  else
    match get_svarint(bs) of
      (v, r) => dec_bytes_go(buf_push(acc, v), r, n - 1)

instance serializeBytes : Serialize(Bytes)
  fn encode(b) = enc_bytes(b)
  fn decode(bs) = dec_bytes(bs)

fn enc_option(o : Option(a)) : Bytes given Serialize(a) =
  match o of
    None => wire_byte(0)
    Some(x) => wire_cat(wire_byte(1), encode(x))

fn dec_option(bs : Bytes) : (Option(a), Bytes) given Serialize(a) =
  match wire_uncons(bs) of
    (t, r) =>
      if t == 0 then
        (None, r)
      elif t == 1 then
        match decode(r) of
          (x, r2) => (Some(x), r2)
      else
        fail()

instance serializeOption : Serialize(Option(a)) given Serialize(a)
  fn encode(o) = enc_option(o)
  fn decode(bs) = dec_option(bs)

-- Tuples are anonymous products, so their codec is positional: each component in
-- order, no length or tag, the exact shape a derived record's body takes. A tuple
-- has no nominal constructor to key an instance on, so the compiler keys these on
-- the tuple's arity (`src/tc`: `HeadKey::Tuple`); the bytes are ordinary library
-- code. Decode threads the remaining bytes through each component in turn.
fn enc_pair(p : (a, b)) : Bytes given Serialize(a), Serialize(b) =
  match p of
    (x, y) => wire_cat(encode(x), encode(y))

fn dec_pair(bs : Bytes) : ((a, b), Bytes) given Serialize(a), Serialize(b) =
  match decode(bs) of
    (x, r1) =>
      match decode(r1) of
        (y, r2) => ((x, y), r2)

instance serializePair : Serialize((a, b)) given Serialize(a), Serialize(b)
  fn encode(p) = enc_pair(p)
  fn decode(bs) = dec_pair(bs)

fn enc_triple(p : (a, b, c)) : Bytes given Serialize(a), Serialize(b), Serialize(c) =
  match p of
    (x, y, z) => wire_cat(encode(x), wire_cat(encode(y), encode(z)))

fn dec_triple(bs : Bytes) : ((a, b, c), Bytes) given Serialize(a), Serialize(b), Serialize(c) =
  match decode(bs) of
    (x, r1) =>
      match decode(r1) of
        (y, r2) =>
          match decode(r2) of
            (z, r3) => ((x, y, z), r3)

instance serializeTriple : Serialize((a, b, c)) given Serialize(a), Serialize(b), Serialize(c)
  fn encode(p) = enc_triple(p)
  fn decode(bs) = dec_triple(bs)

-- A map serializes canonically as two parallel lists, its keys then its values,
-- both in ascending key order. This is canonical (two maps that are equal but
-- were built by different insertion orders serialize identically, so they hash
-- equal, which the incremental engine's early cutoff relies on); the parallel
-- form is chosen for that order-independence, not for want of a tuple codec (one
-- now exists above). Decoding zips the lists back and rebuilds the tree with the
-- ambient `Ord(k)`.
fn enc_map(m : Map(k, v, ord)) : Bytes given Serialize(k), Serialize(v) =
  wire_cat(encode(map_keys(m)), encode(map_values(m)))

fn zip_pairs(ks : List(k), vs : List(v)) : List((k, v)) =
  match ks of
    Nil => Nil
    Cons(k, kr) =>
      match vs of
        Nil => Nil
        Cons(v, vr) => Cons((k, v), zip_pairs(kr, vr))

-- The stored-witness stopgap for the implicit ordering path. A map is written in
-- its own `Ord(k)` order; the reader has no brand to check (the explicit branded
-- path is `Data.Ordered`), so instead it checks the one fact the wire preserves:
-- the keys must be strictly ascending under the READER's `Ord(k)`. A map built
-- under a non-canonical ordering and read back where a different `Ord(k)` is
-- canonical arrives out of order and faults here, deterministically and
-- identically on both backends, rather than silently rebuilding a mis-ordered
-- tree. Same ordering on both sides: the keys are already sorted, so the check is
-- one linear pass the O(n) decode already affords. This closes the implicit hole
-- dynamically where an ordered container crosses a package boundary; a later
-- dictionary-reflection capability closes it statically.
fn keys_strictly_ascending(ks : List(k)) : Bool given Ord(k) =
  match ks of
    Nil => true
    Cons(_, Nil) => true
    Cons(a, Cons(b, r)) => cmp(a, b) < 0 && keys_strictly_ascending(Cons(b, r))

fn dec_map(bs : Bytes) : (Map(k, v, ord), Bytes) given Ord(k), Serialize(k), Serialize(v) =
  match decode(bs) of
    (ks, r1) =>
      match decode(r1) of
        (vs, r2) =>
          guard(keys_strictly_ascending(ks))
          (map_from_list(zip_pairs(ks, vs)), r2)

instance serializeMap : Serialize(Map(k, v, ord)) given Ord(k), Serialize(k), Serialize(v)
  fn encode(m) = enc_map(m)
  fn decode(bs) = dec_map(bs)

-- The envelope. Every serialized thing is one frame:
--
--     [ scheme tag ][ kind ][ contract digest ][ body? ]
--
-- The scheme tag governs the whole wire; a scheme bump migrates every kind in one
-- motion. The kind names what the digest identifies. The contract digest is the
-- shape digest of the expected layout, checked before the body. The body is
-- optional: a frame with no body is a pure reference (the peer resolves the digest
-- from its store), a frame with a body inlines the value. Reference and inline are
-- the same frame, told apart only by whether any bytes follow the digest.

-- The scheme tag on every hash in the tree (`src/core/hash.rs::SCHEME`). Pinned
-- here as the wire library's single home for it, checked against the compiler
-- constant by the `library_hook_names_resolve_to_module_definitions` drift guard
-- in `src/names.rs`.

-- | The scheme tag stamped on every frame; a foreign scheme is rejected before
-- anything else in the envelope is read.
--
-- ```prism
-- wire_scheme_tag
-- ```
-- ```output
-- prism-core-hash-v2
-- ```
pub let wire_scheme_tag : String = "prism-core-hash-v2"

-- The five reserved kinds. `value` is implemented now; `def`, `protocol`, `kont`,
-- and `cert` are reserved so the frame shape exists before their bodies do.

-- | The frame kind for an inline or referenced value (the one implemented today).
--
-- ```prism
-- wire_kind_value
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 0
-- ```
pub let wire_kind_value : Int = 0

-- | The reserved frame kind naming a definition by its digest.
pub let wire_kind_def : Int = 1

-- | The reserved frame kind naming a protocol by its digest.
pub let wire_kind_protocol : Int = 2

-- | The reserved frame kind naming a continuation by its digest.
pub let wire_kind_kont : Int = 3

-- | The reserved frame kind naming a certificate by its digest.
pub let wire_kind_cert : Int = 4

-- A length-prefixed string, reusing the `String` codec, for the scheme tag and
-- the digest inside a frame.
fn put_frame_str(s : String) : Bytes = encode(s)

fn get_frame_str(bs : Bytes) : (String, Bytes) = decode(bs)

-- | Build a frame around a body. `wire_ref` builds the bodyless reference form.
--
-- ```prism
-- bytes_to_list(wire_open(wire_frame(wire_kind_value, "dig", bytes_of_list([7, 8])), wire_kind_value, "dig"))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- [7, 8]
-- ```
pub fn wire_frame(kind : Int, digest : String, body : Bytes) : Bytes =
  wire_cat(
      put_frame_str(wire_scheme_tag),
      wire_cat(wire_tag(kind), wire_cat(put_frame_str(digest), body)),
    )

-- | A pure reference: a frame that carries its contract digest and no body. Its
-- identity is the digest; a peer resolves the body from its store or requests it.
--
-- ```prism
-- wire_is_reference(wire_ref(wire_kind_value, "d"), wire_kind_value, "d")
-- ```
-- ```output
-- true
-- ```
pub fn wire_ref(kind : Int, digest : String) : Bytes =
  wire_frame(kind, digest, wire_empty)

-- | Open a frame, checking the scheme, kind, and digest before the body and
-- returning the body bytes that follow. Any header mismatch fails through `Fail`,
-- so a stale layout is rejected on a cheap comparison, never by a corrupt field.
pub fn wire_open(bs : Bytes, kind : Int, digest : String) : Bytes =
  match get_frame_str(bs) of
    (scheme, r1) =>
      if scheme == wire_scheme_tag then
        match wire_get_tag(r1) of
          (k, r2) =>
            if k == kind then
              match get_frame_str(r2) of
                (d, r3) =>
                  if d == digest then
                    r3
                  else
                    fail()
            else
              fail()
      else
        fail()

-- | True when a well-formed frame for `kind`/`digest` carries no body (a pure
-- reference). Fails if the header itself does not match.
pub fn wire_is_reference(bs : Bytes, kind : Int, digest : String) : Bool =
  wire_is_empty(wire_open(bs, kind, digest))

-- | Open a `value`-kind frame without knowing its contract digest up front,
-- returning that digest alongside the body bytes. It checks the scheme and the
-- `value` kind before the digest. An empty body is legal and returned as-is: a
-- record with no fields encodes to zero bytes, so emptiness cannot be read as
-- "reference" here without an explicit marker in the frame. Trailing-byte
-- discipline is left to the body decoder, exactly as `wire_open` leaves it. A
-- version-dispatched reader uses the returned digest to pick which frozen rung
-- the body decodes as.
--
-- ```prism
-- fst(wire_open_value_any(wire_frame(wire_kind_value, "dig", wire_empty)))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- dig
-- ```
pub fn wire_open_value_any(bs : Bytes) : (String, Bytes) =
  match get_frame_str(bs) of
    (scheme, r1) =>
      if scheme == wire_scheme_tag then
        match wire_get_tag(r1) of
          (k, r2) =>
            if k == wire_kind_value then
              match get_frame_str(r2) of
                (d, r3) => (d, r3)
            else
              fail()
      else
        fail()

-- | Encode a value as a `value`-kind frame carrying an explicitly supplied contract
-- digest. This is the escape hatch: it trusts the caller's digest verbatim, so it is
-- for code that already holds a compiler-computed digest (a `stable` block's
-- generated frame helpers) or is exercising a hand-built frame in a test. Ordinary
-- `Stable` code uses `wire_encode_stable`, which supplies the digest from the type.
--
-- ```prism
-- (wire_decode_value_with_digest(wire_encode_value_with_digest("d", 42), "d") : Int)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 42
-- ```
pub fn wire_encode_value_with_digest(
  digest : String,
  x : a
) : Bytes given Serialize(a) =
  wire_frame(wire_kind_value, digest, encode(x))

-- | Decode a `value`-kind frame against an explicitly supplied contract digest:
-- check the header, decode the body, and reject trailing bytes. A bodyless reference
-- frame fails here, because a value cannot be materialized without its bytes. The
-- digest-supplying counterpart to `wire_encode_value_with_digest`; ordinary `Stable`
-- code uses `wire_decode_stable`.
pub fn wire_decode_value_with_digest(
  bs : Bytes,
  digest : String
) : a given Serialize(a) =
  match decode(wire_open(bs, wire_kind_value, digest)) of
    (v, rest) =>
      if wire_is_empty(rest) then
        v
      else
        fail()

-- | Encode a `Stable` value as a `value` frame under its own contract digest. The
-- digest is `shape_digest_of`, a per-type constant the `deriving (Stable)` instance
-- carries, so no digest string is hand-threaded. This is the ordinary encode for a
-- frozen-serializable value.
pub fn wire_encode_stable(x : a) : Bytes given Stable(a), Serialize(a) =
  wire_encode_value_with_digest(shape_digest_of(x), x)

-- | Decode a `Stable` value from a `value` frame, checking the frame's digest
-- against the type's own `shape_digest_of` and rejecting trailing bytes. The result
-- type comes from the use site; an unannotated call is ambiguous and asks for an
-- annotation. A wrong digest, a wrong kind, a truncated body, and trailing bytes are
-- all decode failures through `Fail`. The frame is opened without assuming its
-- digest, the body decoded as the annotated type, and only then is the frame's
-- digest required to equal that type's own, so a frame minted for another shape is
-- refused.
pub fn wire_decode_stable(bs : Bytes) : a given Stable(a), Serialize(a) =
  match wire_open_value_any(bs) of
    (dig, body) =>
      match decode(body) of
        (v, rest) =>
          if wire_is_empty(rest) && dig == shape_digest_of(v) then
            v
          else
            fail()

-- The version ladder. Frozen versions are spanned by O(n) adjacent converters
-- composed along the ladder, never the N-squared matrix. `upgrade` is total (it
-- defaults new fields); `downgrade` is partial and honest (it reports the fields
-- it had to drop as a `Loss`). The grammar has no multi-parameter
-- `Migrate(lo, hi)` class syntax, so the ladder is the plain functions composed by
-- the `stable` block desugar.

-- | The empty `Loss`: a downgrade that dropped nothing.
pub let no_loss : Loss = Loss(Nil)

-- | A `Loss` naming the fields a downgrade dropped.
--
-- ```prism
-- loss_names(dropped(["port", "tls"]))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- [port, tls]
-- ```
pub fn dropped(names : List(String)) : Loss = Loss(names)

-- | The field names inside a `Loss`.
pub fn loss_names(l : Loss) : List(String) =
  match l of
    Loss(ns) => ns

-- | True when a `Loss` dropped nothing, so the downgrade was lossless. The safe
-- subset of a version step is exactly the values whose downgrade is lossless.
--
-- ```prism
-- (lossless(no_loss), lossless(dropped(["x"])))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- (true, false)
-- ```
pub fn lossless(l : Loss) : Bool = length(loss_names(l)) == 0

-- | Merge two losses along a composed downgrade.
--
-- ```prism
-- loss_names(loss_union(dropped(["a"]), dropped(["b"])))
-- ```
-- ```output
-- [a, b]
-- ```
pub fn loss_union(a : Loss, b : Loss) : Loss =
  Loss(append(loss_names(a), loss_names(b)))

-- | Compose two adjacent upgrades into one spanning upgrade.
--
-- ```prism
-- compose_upgrade(\(x) -> x + 1, \(y) -> y * 2)(3)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- 8
-- ```
pub fn compose_upgrade(lo_mid : (a) -> b, mid_hi : (b) -> c) : (a) -> c =
  \(x) -> mid_hi(lo_mid(x))

-- | Compose two adjacent downgrades into one spanning downgrade, unioning the
-- losses each step reported.
--
-- ```prism
-- compose_downgrade(\(z) -> (z - 1, dropped(["hi"])), \(m) -> (m, no_loss))(10)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- (9, Wire.Loss([hi]))
-- ```
pub fn compose_downgrade(
  hi_mid : (c) -> (b, Loss),
  mid_lo : (b) -> (a, Loss)
) : (c) -> (a, Loss) =
  \(z) -> match hi_mid(z) of { (m, l1) => match mid_lo(m) of { (x, l2) => (x, loss_union(l1, l2)) } }

-- | How to reconcile a higher-version value that a reader cannot represent at its
-- own version: `Reject` refuses it, `LargestSafeSubset` downgrades it and keeps
-- the `Loss`. A version mismatch always has one of these defined outcomes, never
-- undefined behavior.
pub type Policy = Reject | LargestSafeSubset

-- | Apply a mismatch policy to a downgrade. `Reject` fails through `Fail`;
-- `LargestSafeSubset` runs the downgrade and returns the lowered value with the
-- fields it had to drop.
--
-- ```prism
-- reconcile(LargestSafeSubset, \(x) -> (x - 1, no_loss), 5)
-- ```
-- ```output
-- (4, Wire.Loss([]))
-- ```
pub fn reconcile(p : Policy, down : (hi) -> (lo, Loss), x : hi) : (lo, Loss) =
  match p of
    Reject => fail()
    LargestSafeSubset => down(x)

defs.name: Map
defs.source: type Map(k, v, ord) = Tip | Bin(Int, k, v, Map(k, v, ord), Map(k, v, ord))
defs.doc: A persistent ordered map, an AVL tree (`Tip`/`Bin`); see `Data.Map`. The third parameter `ord` is a phantom brand recording the ordering witness the map was built under; it never appears in a field, so an unbranded `Map(k, v)` is the same type under-applied (a fresh brand per use). See `Data.Map`.

defs.name: Canonical
defs.source: type Canonical = MkCanonical
defs.doc: The brand of a map built under the ambient canonical ordering, when no explicit ordering witness is in scope. A map built inside `with w <- ordering` carries `w`'s private brand instead, so a value of one brand never unifies with the other. Maps stored in a container that pins a concrete brand (rather than staying brand-polymorphic) use this one.

defs.name: int_pow
defs.source:
fn int_pow(base, n) =
  if n < 0 then
    1 / int_pow_go(base, -n, 1)
  else
    int_pow_go(base, n, 1)
defs.doc:
Integer exponentiation, the `Pow(Int)` instance: bignum-correct because `*` promotes past 63 bits, and tail recursive so a large exponent folds in constant stack. `a ^ b` over ints lowers here through the `Pow` class. A negative exponent is defined as `1 / a ^ (-b)` under the language's one truncating division rule: `0` whenever the magnitude of the base exceeds 1, the exact reciprocal for a base of `1` or `-1`, and the division-by-zero fault for a base of `0` (which is exactly what `0 ^ -1` is).

defs.name: Plate
defs.doc:
One layer of a value's own structure, taken apart and put back. `children(x)` is the list of `x`'s immediate subvalues *of `x`'s own type*, in constructor-declaration and field order, and nothing else; `rebuild(x, ks)` is `x` with those same positions replaced, left to right, by the elements of `ks`. A whole-tree traversal (every subterm, a fold, a count, a rewrite) is written once against this one pair instead of once per constructor, so a fifty-constructor syntax tree costs the same to walk as a two-constructor one. `children` is pure and total: an empty effect row, and a list of structurally smaller values, so a recursion driven by `children` terminates on a finite value.

The law every combinator above these two relies on is that they are inverse on one layer: `rebuild(x, children(x))` is `x`, and the list handed to `rebuild` must have the same length and the same order as the one `children` returned. A list of any other length is a programming error, not an input to be repaired: `rebuild` raises `Fail` rather than padding the missing positions or dropping the extra ones, because either repair would hand back a value that is not the one asked for, and would do it silently. That is the whole content of the `Fail` in the row; on a correctly shaped list `rebuild` performs no effect.

`deriving (Plate)` generates both from the declaration, reaching through list, optional, tuple, and record fields, and through the other types declared in the program, to find the occurrences a field can lead to. That is what lets a traversal see through the carrier records a syntax tree holds its nodes in (a match arm, a spanned wrapper, a qualifier) without anyone writing a second match for them.

The derivation is structural rather than compositional, so it differs from the other derived classes in two visible ways. It puts no constraint on the type's parameters, because a `Plate(T(a))` yields `T` occurrences and never an `a`; and it asks nothing of a component's own instances, because it takes the component apart by its declaration rather than by dispatch. A field it cannot take apart, and that could still lead back to the derived type (a function, a container with no declaration in the program), is a compile error at the `deriving` clause naming the field, never a silently dropped subterm. Both methods come from one walk of the declaration, read forwards and backwards, so the derived pair satisfies the law by construction. Unlike `Wire.Stable`, whose method is a compiler-injected constant, nothing here is unforgeable: a hand-written instance is an ordinary instance and is accepted, which is the escape hatch for an abstract type whose children the compiler cannot see, and which is also where the law becomes the author's to keep.

defs.source:

defs.name: escape_at
defs.source:
fn escape_at(c : Int, s : String, i : Int) : String =
  if c == 34 then
    "\\\""
  elif c == 92 then
    "\\\\"
  elif c == 10 then
    "\\n"
  elif c == 9 then
    "\\t"
  elif c == 13 then
    "\\r"
  else
    substring(s, i, 1)
